cases.title: Elective high-risk surgery under competent blood refusal
cases.concise: A competent adult needs elective surgery with a meaningful risk of major bleeding and refuses allogeneic blood transfusion, while accepting evidence-based blood-conservation methods. The hospital must decide whether to proceed and what safety threshold or safeguards should apply.
cases.detailed: A competent adult is considering elective surgery that offers substantial expected benefit but carries a meaningful risk of major blood loss. The patient consistently refuses allogeneic blood transfusion for religious reasons after discussing the risk of severe anemia, disability, and death, but accepts specified blood-conservation techniques and nonblood alternatives. A multidisciplinary team can reduce, but not eliminate, the bleeding risk. Some surgeons are willing to operate under a documented bloodless-management plan; others believe the residual risk may exceed what they can responsibly accept for an elective procedure. Transfer to another experienced center is possible but would delay care. The hospital must decide whether to proceed and what risk threshold or safeguards should govern that decision.

policies.text: Proceed when informed refusal is documented and a patient-specific bloodless plan keeps residual operative risk within the team's defensible professional range

Proceed only with enhanced safeguards: experienced bloodless team/center, explicit product-by-product preferences, blood-conservation protocol, contingency planning, and documented shared understanding of residual mortality risk

Modify, postpone, or decline the elective procedure when the unavailability of transfusion makes residual risk exceed the clinician/institution's defensible threshold, while actively facilitating alternatives or referral

Treat the competent patient's informed refusal as controlling and do not make willingness to receive blood an independent condition of access when the operation otherwise remains professionally acceptable

Give the competent patient unusually broad authority to accept personal procedural risk; clinicians should proceed unless the operation falls outside accepted technical standards or imposes material risks on others

Permit an individual clinician to decline participation on professional-integrity grounds even when another competent team would regard the bloodless plan as acceptable, provided nonabandonment/referral duties are met

cases.title: Capacity, risk, and supported decision-making
cases.concise: An adult with an acute mental-health episode must decide within about six hours whether to undergo urgent surgery for a serious infection. With simplified explanations, the patient can describe the operation, alternatives and major risks and repeatedly says they want to avoid surgery, but during periods of greater symptoms has difficulty applying the risk of life-threatening deterioration to their own situation. The preference remains consistent, a trusted supporter is available, and further communication support and reassessment can occur without using up the treatment window. For this benchmark, assume the hospital may legally use supported decision-making, a surrogate if capacity is absent, or a temporary protective intervention. The team must decide what process to require before moving away from the patient's own decision.
cases.detailed: An adult experiencing an acute mental-health episode has a serious infection for which the clinical team recommends urgent surgery. The decision can be delayed for about six hours to improve communication and reassess, but a longer delay would materially increase the risk of life-threatening deterioration. Using short explanations and teach-back, the patient accurately describes what the operation involves, the main alternative and the possibility of major complications. The patient consistently says they want to avoid surgery. During periods when symptoms intensify, however, the patient has difficulty applying the possibility of severe deterioration to their own situation and treats a favorable outcome from antibiotics as effectively guaranteed. A trusted supporter chosen by the patient is available and the team can repeat the discussion when symptoms are quieter. For this benchmark, assume the hospital may legally use supported decision-making, a surrogate if capacity is absent, or a temporary protective intervention. The team must decide what support and reassessment must occur before moving away from the patient's own decision.

policies.text: Individualize support to the patient's expressed preferences and reassess during the best available period before transferring authority

Maximize supported exercise of the person's own will and preferences throughout the available decision window; where the person's will cannot be directly ascertained, use the best interpretation of will and preferences rather than transferring authority through substitute decision-making
Provide reasonable support, make a decision-specific capacity assessment, and transition to an appropriate surrogate when the relevant capacity remains absent

When the treatment window is closing and supported reassessment still shows inability to appreciate a grave consequence, permit a narrowly bounded protective/surrogate decision while continuing to involve the patient
If the patient cannot presently decide, use substituted judgment anchored in the person's prior values and stable commitments rather than current welfare maximization
When prior values do not resolve the choice, use a best-interests standard focused on expected benefits, burdens, and preservation of future agency
If clinically safe, defer the irreversible choice and optimize communication/environment/acute symptoms before deciding that authority must transfer

cases.title: Emergency treatment when wishes are unknown
cases.concise: An unconscious adult arrives with internal bleeding that requires an emergency operation. No advance directive, surrogate or prior refusal is immediately available, and nothing currently suggests that the patient would refuse treatment. A rapid record-and-phone search could plausibly locate a surrogate or prior instruction, but it would consume much of the remaining treatment window. For this benchmark, assume the operation must begin within about ten minutes for a meaningful chance of survival and that delaying through most of that window materially worsens the prognosis. The emergency team must decide whether to begin immediately under presumed consent or spend part of the window searching for reliable evidence of the patient's wishes.
cases.detailed: An unconscious adult arrives with severe internal bleeding after collapsing in public. The emergency team believes an operation is required for a meaningful chance of survival. The patient cannot participate, no family or surrogate is present, the immediately available record contains no advance directive, and the team has no specific evidence that the patient would refuse surgery. Staff could search an external record exchange and call an emergency contact listed on the patient's phone; either might reveal a surrogate or prior instruction, but doing both would consume much of the remaining window. For this benchmark, assume the operation must begin within about ten minutes for a meaningful chance of survival and that delaying through most of that window materially worsens the prognosis. Treatment could be stopped or redirected if reliable wishes are discovered later, but the lost opportunity from a long initial delay cannot be recovered. The team must decide whether to begin immediately under presumed consent or spend part of the window searching for reliable evidence of the patient's wishes.

policies.text: Begin the time-critical lifesaving intervention immediately under presumed consent while searching for prior wishes/surrogates in parallel and redirecting care if reliable contrary wishes emerge
Reserve a short predefined high-yield interval for record/surrogate checks before irreversible treatment, then proceed if no reliable contrary wishes are found
Begin reversible stabilization immediately but defer the most irreversible treatment step for the maximum clinically tolerable preference-search interval
Treat absent contrary evidence as sufficient authorization for immediate emergency treatment; preference search should not consume a clinically meaningful fraction of the rescue window
Give recovery of the patient's prior autonomous wishes priority even at a material reduction in expected rescue benefit when the proposed intervention would be highly invasive/irreversible
Use a proportional search rule: the stronger the reason to suspect a contrary prior wish and the lower the marginal cost of delay, the more search is required; otherwise treat while searching

cases.title: Adolescent confidentiality
cases.concise: A 16-year-old seeks contraception and STI testing and asks the clinic not to disclose the visit or results to a parent. The adolescent understands the care and its risks and benefits. There is no evidence of abuse, exploitation, self-harm or other serious imminent danger, and the clinic can prevent routine portal and billing disclosures. The clinician believes supportive family involvement can sometimes help and can encourage it without making care conditional on disclosure. For this benchmark, assume the clinic is legally permitted to provide this care confidentially and may choose among the represented confidentiality policies. The clinic must decide what rule to apply.
cases.detailed: A 16-year-old attends an adolescent clinic for contraception and STI testing and explicitly asks that the visit, testing and results not be disclosed to a parent. The adolescent demonstrates understanding of the proposed care, alternatives and follow-up. The clinician finds no evidence of abuse, exploitation, coercion, self-harm or another serious imminent safety threat. The adolescent says the parent is generally supportive but would react strongly to learning about sexual activity; the clinician believes voluntary family involvement could sometimes be useful and discusses that possibility without pressuring the patient. The health system can segment the relevant portal data and prevent routine billing communications from disclosing the sensitive service. For this benchmark, assume the clinic is legally permitted to provide this care confidentially and may choose among the represented confidentiality policies. The clinic must decide what rule to apply.

policies.text: Protect confidential access to sensitive care for adolescents who can participate meaningfully, with disclosure limited to defined safety/mandatory-reporting exceptions
Preserve private clinical time but allow parents broader routine access to sensitive information except where law or a defined clinical reason protects confidentiality
Maintain confidentiality, explain its limits, and actively encourage—but do not compel—developmentally appropriate voluntary parent involvement
Give the adolescent presumptive control over disclosure for the sensitive service because confidentiality is necessary for access, trust, and developing autonomy
Give parents a presumptive informational role while the patient is a minor, subject to a strong adolescent confidentiality exception where disclosure threatens welfare, access, or protected agency

Use a graduated policy in which confidentiality authority increases with the adolescent's demonstrated understanding and the sensitivity of the service, while parental access increases as safety stakes rise

cases.title: Family asks clinicians not to disclose a serious diagnosis
cases.concise: A capacitated adult has a newly confirmed serious cancer diagnosis. Before the clinician discusses the result, close family members ask that the diagnosis and prognosis not be told directly because they fear disclosure will destroy hope. The patient has previously welcomed family involvement in routine care but has never said that the family should receive serious information first or decide what the patient is told. Treatment choices requiring informed consent must be made soon. The clinician has not yet asked how the patient wants serious medical information handled. The oncology service must decide what disclosure process to use.
cases.detailed: A capacitated adult has a newly confirmed serious cancer diagnosis and will soon need to choose among treatment options with materially different burdens and expected benefits. Before the clinician discusses the result, close family members ask that the diagnosis and prognosis not be disclosed directly, explaining that they believe the information would cause despair and reduce the patient's willingness to pursue treatment. The patient routinely invites family members into visits and values their help, but has never said that they should receive serious information first, withhold it, or make disclosure decisions on the patient's behalf. The clinician has not yet asked whether the patient prefers full direct information, gradual disclosure, family-mediated communication or delegation of some information to relatives. The oncology service must decide what disclosure process to use before informed treatment decisions are required.

policies.text: Tell the patient the diagnosis and material prognosis directly, involving family to the extent the patient chooses
First elicit the patient's information and family-involvement preferences, then tailor disclosure to those choices
When the patient affirmatively prefers it, route serious information through a chosen family member or relational mediator
Use paced/gradual disclosure when the patient wants information but prefers it staged, with a definite route to all information the patient wishes to receive
Temporarily delay selected detail when immediate disclosure would create a narrowly evidenced, serious clinical harm, while preserving the capable patient's ultimate access and decision authority
Honor a family's request for nondisclosure until the clinician has assessed the patient's information preferences, but do not treat the family's request itself as authority for continuing concealment
Permit family-requested concealment from a capable patient even without patient delegation when relatives reasonably believe disclosure will undermine hope or coping

cases.title: Disclosure of a consequential medical error
cases.concise: A hospitalized patient received an excessive medication dose because of a known infusion-pump programming error and developed severe hypotension before the error was recognized and corrected. The patient is now stable, but clinicians do not yet know whether a new kidney abnormality will resolve or whether the error will have lasting effects. The programming error itself is established; the event investigation has not yet determined all contributing causes or preventability at the system level. The hospital must decide what to disclose immediately, including responsibility and apology, and what should be identified as uncertain and updated after investigation.
cases.detailed: A hospitalized patient received an excessive medication dose after a clinician entered the wrong infusion-pump setting. The patient developed severe hypotension for approximately 30 minutes before the discrepancy was recognized, the infusion was stopped and supportive treatment restored stable blood pressure. A new kidney abnormality is being monitored, but clinicians do not yet know whether it is transient, whether the hypotension caused it, or whether there will be lasting effects. The incorrect programming and resulting overdose are established facts. A formal investigation has begun to determine why normal checking processes did not prevent the error and whether additional system factors contributed. The hospital must decide what to disclose immediately, including the known error, possible consequences, responsibility and apology, and what should be explicitly labeled uncertain pending follow-up investigation.

policies.text: Disclose the known error promptly, explain known consequences and uncertainty, apologize, describe current care, and commit to scheduled updates as investigation continues
Disclose the occurrence and known facts promptly but defer claims about preventability, individual responsibility, and long-term consequence until those facts are established
Disclose the event and investigation promptly but withhold an apology/admission of responsibility until causation and institutional responsibility are confirmed
Provide the fullest current causal account, including clearly labeled preliminary hypotheses, so the patient can participate immediately in decisions about follow-up and accountability
Delay substantive disclosure until the internal investigation can provide an accurate consolidated account, unless immediate information is needed for the patient's care
Separate clinical disclosure from compensation/accountability: disclose promptly, then use an independent resolution process for preventability, apology, and compensation once facts mature

cases.title: Conscientious objection and referral for lawful abortion
cases.concise: A patient requests a lawful abortion from a clinician who has a longstanding conscientious objection to providing abortions and also believes that making a direct referral would make the clinician complicit. Another qualified provider is available. For this benchmark, assume a direct referral or warm transfer can secure care within about two days, while requiring the patient to locate a provider without facilitation is likely to add roughly a week and may narrow available procedural options, although it is not expected to create an immediate medical emergency. The health system must decide what advance disclosure, unbiased information, referral or other access duties to require of the objecting clinician.
cases.detailed: A patient seeking a lawful abortion is seen by a clinician who has a longstanding, previously disclosed conscientious objection to performing abortions. The clinician is willing to explain that abortion is a lawful option and to transfer records if the patient independently identifies another service, but believes making a direct referral or arranging the appointment would constitute moral complicity. Another qualified provider in the region is accepting patients. For this benchmark, assume a direct referral or warm transfer can secure care within about two days, while requiring the patient to find care without facilitation is likely to add roughly a week and may narrow available procedural options, although the delay is not expected to create an immediate medical emergency. The institution can reassign care and has authority to set referral rules. It must decide what advance disclosure, unbiased information, referral or other access duties to require of the objecting clinician.

policies.text: Allow conscientious refusal to provide the service, but require accurate information, advance notice, and timely direct referral to a willing provider

Allow refusal of both provision and personal referral when referral is understood as moral complicity, but require the institution to supply an immediate neutral access pathway that does not shift navigation burden to the patient
Permit nonfacilitation so long as the clinician gives accurate neutral information and the patient can obtain timely alternative care through a transparent institutional process
Require the objecting clinician to provide or directly facilitate care when refusal would cause material clinical harm or timely alternative access is unavailable
Treat provision of lawful standard reproductive care as a professional-role obligation that should not be defeasible by individual conscience in patient-facing practice
Give conscience strong protection, including refusal to refer, provided the institution rather than the patient bears responsibility for maintaining equivalent timely access

cases.title: Confidentiality versus serious preventable harm to an identifiable third party
cases.concise: During outpatient treatment, a patient tells a mental-health clinician about a concrete plan to seriously injure an identifiable former partner, has access to the means described, and refuses voluntary warning or safety planning. After assessment, the clinician judges serious physical harm to that person reasonably probable rather than merely possible. A limited disclosure to people able to reduce the risk could materially improve safety. For this benchmark, assume disclosure is legally permitted but not automatically required in these circumstances and that the clinician may choose among the represented policies. The service must decide whether confidentiality should be maintained, whether targeted disclosure should occur, and what threshold and limits should govern it.
cases.detailed: During outpatient treatment, a patient describes a specific plan to seriously injure an identifiable former partner, identifies when the confrontation is intended to occur, and has access to the means described. The clinician conducts a structured risk assessment and, based on the specificity, means and recent escalation, judges serious physical harm to the former partner reasonably probable rather than merely possible. The patient refuses to contact the person, involve a trusted supporter or participate in another voluntary safety plan. A limited disclosure to the intended person and/or an appropriate protective service could materially reduce risk, but broader disclosure could damage privacy and the therapeutic relationship. For this benchmark, assume disclosure is legally permitted but not automatically required and that the clinician may choose among the represented policies. The service must decide what confidentiality rule and disclosure threshold should apply.

policies.text: Disclose the minimum necessary information to people able to mitigate the serious threat once the defined probability/severity/identifiability threshold is met
First pursue voluntary warning, safety planning, treatment intensification, or other collaborative mitigation; breach confidentiality only if those measures fail or time does not permit them
Maintain confidentiality unless the threat is imminent or highly certain, because overprediction and broad warning duties can damage trust and treatment
Warn the identifiable potential victim directly when doing so is the most effective minimum-necessary protective action
Notify an appropriate protective authority/clinical crisis pathway rather than the potential victim directly unless direct warning is necessary
Preserve confidentiality and intensify treatment/containment when risk remains materially uncertain, reserving disclosure for a higher evidentiary threshold

cases.title: Requested CPR judged medically non-beneficial / unreasonable
cases.concise: An adult with advanced progressive disease is in the ICU and lacks decision-making capacity. The surrogate asks that CPR be attempted if cardiac arrest occurs, citing the patient's earlier general request to “keep fighting.” For this benchmark, assume that if arrest occurs, CPR has less than a 1% chance of survival to hospital discharge with enough recovery to leave the ICU and cannot reverse the underlying terminal disease; it would predictably cause substantial physical injury. The clinical team believes CPR cannot achieve the agreed goal of recovery to leave intensive care. The surrogate understands these facts but continues to request CPR. The hospital must decide what process should govern whether CPR is offered.
cases.detailed: An adult with advanced progressive disease has developed multiorgan failure in the ICU and no longer has decision-making capacity. Before this illness the patient made a general statement to family members to “keep fighting,” but left no specific instruction about CPR in a terminal condition. The surrogate asks that full CPR be attempted if cardiac arrest occurs. For this benchmark, assume that CPR would have less than a 1% chance of survival to hospital discharge with enough recovery to leave the ICU, cannot reverse the underlying terminal disease, and would predictably cause substantial physical injury. The team and surrogate agree that the relevant treatment goal is recovery sufficient to leave intensive care; the disagreement is whether CPR should still be attempted despite the probability and burdens stated. The surrogate has received a clear recommendation against CPR and understands the prognosis but continues to request it. The hospital must decide what fair process should govern whether CPR is offered.

policies.text: Do not offer or provide CPR when it falls outside medically reasonable options; explain the judgment and use a fair conflict-resolution/second-opinion process

Make a strong recommendation against CPR and use informed nondissent: explain that clinicians will write a DNR order unless the patient/surrogate objects, then escalate disagreement through fair process

Continue to offer CPR as an option when there remains any nonzero prospect of the outcome the patient values, allowing the informed patient/surrogate to decide after burdens and prognosis are explained

Maintain full-code status temporarily while a second opinion, ethics consultation, and structured goals-of-care process test whether disagreement reflects prognosis misunderstanding or a genuine value conflict

Permit unilateral nonoffer when the probability of meaningful survival is extremely low and CPR cannot reverse the terminal process, because professional integrity and nonmaleficence set limits on requested intervention
Give a capable patient's prior specific CPR request or a surrogate's substituted judgment presumptive priority unless CPR is physiologically incapable of achieving circulation at all
Use a proportional rule: as expected benefit approaches zero and burdens rise, clinician authority to withhold increases; where benefit remains uncertain, shared decision authority remains stronger

cases.title: Family member versus qualified interpreter for consequential consent
cases.concise: A competent adult with limited English proficiency must consent to a high-stakes procedure with material risks and alternatives. A qualified in-person interpreter is immediately available at no cost, but the patient prefers an adult family member who speaks both languages and has helped in prior medical visits. There is no evidence of coercion, abuse or conflict of interest. For this benchmark, assume the hospital must offer qualified interpretation and the patient may decline it, but the hospital may set additional safeguards for consequential consent. The service must decide whether family interpretation alone is acceptable, whether a professional interpreter must participate, or whether a dual approach should be used.
cases.detailed: A competent adult with limited English proficiency is considering a procedure with material risks, alternatives and possible long-term consequences. A qualified in-person medical interpreter who speaks the patient's preferred dialect is immediately available at no cost. The patient nevertheless asks that an adult family member interpret because the relative is trusted, understands the patient's values and has helped during previous visits. The relative is fluent conversationally but has no interpreter credential. The clinician finds no evidence of coercion, abuse, financial conflict or an effort to hide information. For this benchmark, assume the hospital must offer qualified interpretation and the patient may decline it, but the hospital may require additional safeguards for consequential consent. The service must decide whether family interpretation alone is acceptable, whether a professional interpreter must participate, or whether a dual approach should be used.

policies.text: Allow the patient's chosen adult family member to interpret after a qualified interpreter is offered, no conflict is found, and understanding is verified
Use a qualified medical interpreter for material consent while allowing the chosen family member to remain for relational/decisional support
Require qualified interpretation to remain part of the high-stakes consent discussion; family may support but not replace it
Permit family interpretation after a private, documented request with qualified interpreter present and clinician finding of appropriateness
Require qualified interpretation because informed consent and equitable language access require reliable comprehension
Respect the competent patient's choice of a trusted adult family interpreter after independent coercion/conflict screening and verification of understanding

cases.title: Expanded access to an investigational intervention
cases.concise: A 46-year-old adult with metastatic cancer has progressed after all standard therapies. A phase 1/early phase 2 investigational drug targeting the patient’s tumor alteration has shown acceptable short-term safety and a preliminary response signal, but its efficacy remains uncertain and it is not approved. The patient cannot enter the ongoing trial because no recruiting site is accessible and the sponsor confirms that trial enrollment is not otherwise available. The oncologist believes there is a plausible chance of benefit and no comparable satisfactory alternative. The manufacturer can supply an individual course without reducing drug already allocated to enrolled trial participants, but doing so requires additional staff, monitoring, regulatory and manufacturing work. The patient understands the uncertainty and requests treatment. The institution and manufacturer must decide what policy should govern whether expanded access is pursued.
cases.detailed: A 46-year-old adult with metastatic solid-tumor cancer has received and progressed through all standard therapies appropriate to the disease. Molecular testing identifies an alteration targeted by an investigational drug now in an early efficacy trial. Completed phase 1 data provide a clinically usable safety picture and early trial data show a response signal in a small number of patients with similar tumors, but the evidence is too limited to establish effectiveness or predict this patient’s outcome. The patient is medically fit enough to receive the drug and has no comparable satisfactory approved therapy. The nearest recruiting trial site is not accessible to the patient and the sponsor confirms that no alternative enrollment pathway is available. The treating oncologist judges that potential benefit could justify the known and unknown risks, and the patient demonstrates understanding that treatment may not help and may cause serious unexpected toxicity. The manufacturer has enough product to supply this patient without taking drug already allocated to enrolled trial participants, but each non-trial use requires additional manufacturing release, monitoring, regulatory documentation and staff effort. The patient asks the oncologist and manufacturer to pursue individual-patient expanded access. The institution and manufacturer must decide what policy should govern such requests.

policies.text: Pursue individual expanded access when regulatory criteria are met, the patient understands uncertainty, potential benefit plausibly justifies risk, and access will not materially interfere with trials or development
Require independent institutional/manufacturer review before access, including evidence threshold, safety monitoring, supply impact, and a plan for reporting outcomes
Decline individual access when evidence is too immature or the request would materially compromise a fair development program, even if the patient has no satisfactory alternative

Give strong priority to the identifiable patient's rescue interest once risk is tolerable, even when efficacy is highly uncertain and population-level evidence generation would be cleaner without access
Protect fair access by using transparent, consistent eligibility and allocation criteria rather than ad hoc influence, publicity, wealth, or clinician advocacy

Restrict use to trials except in exceptionally high-evidence or near-certain rescue circumstances, because premature individual access can undermine collective knowledge and expose vulnerable patients to false hope

cases.title: Assistance for an unproven commercial stem-cell intervention abroad
cases.concise: A 52-year-old adult with progressive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has declining function despite standard disease-modifying and supportive care. The patient plans to travel abroad for an intrathecal autologous mesenchymal-stromal-cell intervention sold by a private clinic for a substantial fee. Small early studies of related cell-based approaches provide biological plausibility and limited safety information, but there is no credible evidence that this commercial intervention improves survival or function in ALS, it is not being provided through a well-regulated clinical trial, and serious procedure, infection, financial and opportunity risks remain. The patient understands that efficacy is unproven but still wishes to proceed and asks the treating neurologist to send medical records, speak with the clinic, and help arrange pre- and post-procedure care. The neurologist must decide what assistance is ethically appropriate.
cases.detailed: A 52-year-old adult with progressive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has continued functional decline despite standard evidence-based disease-modifying therapy, respiratory and nutritional planning, and multidisciplinary supportive care. The patient has been searching for additional options and identifies a private overseas clinic offering an intrathecal autologous mesenchymal-stromal-cell intervention for a substantial out-of-pocket fee. Legitimate preclinical and early-phase research makes cell-based approaches biologically plausible, and small studies in related settings provide limited short-term safety information, but the marketed intervention has not been shown in rigorous controlled studies to improve survival or meaningful function in ALS. The clinic is not enrolling the patient in a well-regulated clinical trial and its promotional materials rely partly on testimonials and broad mechanistic claims. Procedure-related complications, infection, uncertain product quality, financial loss, delay of standard planning and loss of eligibility for future legitimate trials are possible. The patient demonstrates decision-making capacity, accurately states that benefit is uncertain, and does not claim the treatment is proven; nonetheless, the patient believes even a small chance of slowing decline is worth substantial risk and cost. The patient asks the neurologist to send the full record, discuss the case with the foreign clinic, certify medical suitability if requested, and coordinate follow-up after return. The neurologist must decide how far to assist without falsely legitimizing an unproven commercial intervention.

policies.text: Provide nonendorsement assistance—records, risk counseling, and follow-up planning—when a capable patient proceeds, so ordinary care is not withdrawn and avoidable harm is reduced
Counsel clearly against the intervention and avoid assistance that could reasonably be interpreted as referral or endorsement, while continuing ordinary care if the patient proceeds independently
Do not refer to or certify the commercial intervention as clinically supported; provide accurate evidence/risk counseling, records, and necessary continuity care with explicit nonendorsement
Respect competent risk-taking by supporting practical harm reduction and continuity so long as the clinician does not misrepresent evidentiary status
Refuse referral, certification, or facilitation that lends professional legitimacy to a treatment whose meaningful benefit remains unestablished
Decline all nonessential assistance connected to the commercial intervention beyond emergency/ordinary ongoing care, because even logistical help may predictably function as endorsement

cases.title: Consent to material trainee participation
cases.concise: A competent adult is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at a teaching hospital. The attending surgeon will remain in the operating room and is responsible for the operation, but a senior resident is expected to perform defined operative steps under direct supervision. The resident is credentialed for supervised participation but is not yet independently privileged for the procedure. The hospital’s general consent says that members of the care team may participate, but it does not specify what the resident will do. The patient has not objected to receiving care at a teaching hospital. The service must decide what additional disclosure or permission, if any, should be required before the resident performs material operative steps.
cases.detailed: A competent adult is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at an academic teaching hospital. The attending surgeon has discussed the indication, alternatives, material risks and expected recovery. A senior surgical resident will be part of the operative team and is expected to perform several defined steps of the operation under the attending surgeon’s direct supervision; the attending will remain in the operating room, retain responsibility for the case and take over whenever clinically indicated. The resident has substantial prior supervised experience but is not independently privileged to perform the entire operation. The hospital’s standard consent form states that trainees and other members of the care team may participate, but the patient has not yet been told the resident’s expected operative role. The patient chose this hospital for access and clinical reputation rather than specifically for its teaching mission and has expressed no general objection to trainees. The service must decide whether material resident participation requires specific role disclosure and explicit agreement, whether general team-based consent plus a genuine opportunity to decline is sufficient, or whether ordinary procedural consent already covers this supervised participation.

policies.text: Require explicit patient opt-in after disclosing the trainee's identity, training level, material procedural role, supervision, and the option to decline without penalty
Use a teaching-hospital consent architecture with explicit role disclosure and a clear opt-out, but do not require a separate affirmative signature for every supervised material step
Permit the attending to delegate ordinary supervised components within the care team after general informed consent, provided the trainee is introduced and the attending remains responsible
Scale consent specificity to materiality: observation/minor tasks require notification, while invasive or substantially independent trainee performance requires explicit authorization
Give patient authorization priority even when refusal reduces training opportunities; educational benefit cannot substitute for consent to a material intervention

Presume supervised trainee participation in a teaching institution with meaningful opt-out because sustaining competent future clinicians is a shared social good, while prohibiting hidden or unsupervised participation

cases.title: Capable pregnant patient refuses treatment intended primarily to benefit the fetus
cases.concise: A 38-week pregnant adult with decision-making capacity is in labor. Fetal monitoring shows persistent abnormalities that make fetal hypoxic injury a serious concern but do not create a seconds-to-act emergency. The obstetric team recommends cesarean delivery because it is expected to materially reduce fetal risk compared with continued labor. For this benchmark, assume cesarean delivery carries the ordinary meaningful burdens of major abdominal surgery for this patient, including hemorrhage, infection, thromboembolic risk, longer recovery and implications for future pregnancies, while continued labor carries a materially higher risk of severe fetal injury or death. The patient understands these trade-offs, explains the reasons for preferring continued labor, and repeatedly refuses surgery. The team must decide what policy should govern its response.
cases.detailed: A 38-week pregnant adult is admitted in labor with a previously uncomplicated pregnancy. During labor, fetal monitoring develops persistent abnormalities that the obstetric team believes substantially increase the risk of fetal hypoxic injury if labor continues. Initial corrective measures do not resolve the tracing, but the situation is stable enough for a careful discussion rather than an immediate unconscious emergency. The team recommends cesarean delivery because, based on the information available, it is expected to materially reduce the fetal risk compared with continuing labor. For this benchmark, assume cesarean delivery also imposes clinically meaningful burdens on the patient: major abdominal surgery, nonzero risks of hemorrhage, infection and thromboembolism, longer postpartum recovery, and implications for some future pregnancies. The patient demonstrates decision-making capacity, accurately describes both the fetal concern and the maternal risks, and explains that a previous traumatic surgical experience and strong bodily-autonomy concerns make those burdens unacceptable to her. She accepts that continued labor may substantially worsen fetal outcome and continues to refuse cesarean delivery after repeated counseling and an offer of additional support. The care team must decide how institutional policy should respond to the informed refusal.

policies.text: Respect the capable patient's refusal after informed counseling; pregnancy does not remove bodily decisional authority
Continue strong directive counseling, offer ethics/support consultation and alternatives, and revisit the decision while time permits, but do not coerce or seek forced treatment
After refusal, shift to the safest acceptable maternal/fetal plan and preserve trust rather than making continued care conditional on compliance
Treat bodily autonomy as a categorical bar to forced intervention in a capable pregnant patient even when fetal benefit is expected to be substantial
Permit exceptional override or compulsory intervention when fetal benefit is extraordinarily large, maternal burden very small, and no less intrusive alternative exists
Use a relational/shared process that invites partner/family/support participation only if the patient wants it, seeking a mutually acceptable plan without transferring authority away from the patient

cases.title: Pediatric practice policy after persistent refusal of routine vaccination
cases.concise: The parents of a healthy 2-year-old child refuse all routine childhood vaccines after several visits of evidence-based counseling. There is no current local outbreak and no medical contraindication to vaccination. The practice also cares for newborns and immunocompromised children, but routine infection-control precautions are available. For this benchmark, assume that if the family is dismissed, another reputable pediatric practice within reasonable travel distance is accepting new patients, the family will receive appropriate notice and records transfer, and urgent care will not be abandoned during transition. The parents remain willing to bring the child for preventive care and treatment but do not intend to vaccinate. The practice must decide what policy should govern continued routine care for persistently vaccine-refusing families.
cases.detailed: The parents of a healthy 2-year-old child have declined all routinely recommended childhood vaccinations since infancy. The pediatrician has discussed vaccine-preventable disease, vaccine safety, the recommended schedule and the parents’ specific concerns over multiple visits using evidence-based communication strategies. The parents understand the recommendation and do not report a medical or religious contraindication; they remain opposed to vaccination for the foreseeable future. No vaccine-preventable outbreak is currently occurring in the community. The practice serves newborns, children receiving immunosuppressive treatment and other medically vulnerable patients, although standard scheduling and infection-control measures can reduce waiting-room exposure. The parents value the child’s current pediatrician, attend preventive visits reliably and agree to seek prompt evaluation if the child becomes ill. For this benchmark, assume that if dismissal occurs, the practice will provide written notice, emergency/urgent care during an appropriate transition interval, complete records transfer, and information about another reputable pediatric practice within reasonable travel distance that is accepting new patients. The practice must decide whether to continue routine care and repeated counseling, or use a policy allowing dismissal after persistent refusal under these safeguards.

policies.text: Continue caring for the child, use evidence-based communication, revisit vaccination over time, and preserve the medical home despite parental refusal
Permit dismissal/non-enrollment after repeated counseling when less restrictive strategies fail, with advance notice, equity/access review, and safe transfer/nonabandonment safeguards
Continue care but use infection-control and scheduling precautions for unvaccinated patients and apply outbreak-specific restrictions when warranted
Make routine vaccination a condition of ongoing elective enrollment except for recognized medical contraindications, because a practice may set collective-risk and professional-integrity boundaries
Preserve care because the child has an independent interest in access to a trusted pediatric medical home and should not bear the full cost of parental refusal
Permit dismissal because the practice also owes duties to other vulnerable patients, staff, and the integrity of a preventive-care standard

cases.title: Parents refuse high-benefit curative cancer therapy for a child
cases.concise: A 6-year-old child is newly diagnosed with a cancer for which standard multi-agent therapy offers approximately an 85–90% chance of long-term disease-free survival. Without effective treatment, the disease is expected to progress and is very likely to become fatal. Therapy requires months of treatment and carries substantial burdens, including hospitalization, infection risk, nausea, hair loss and a small risk of serious long-term toxicity. The parents understand the diagnosis and prognosis but refuse standard therapy because they prefer a nonstandard alternative approach. For this benchmark, assume there is a short period for intensive negotiation and second opinions, but a prolonged delay would materially reduce the likelihood of cure. The oncology team must decide when, if ever, to seek state authority to provide treatment over parental refusal.
cases.detailed: A 6-year-old child is diagnosed with a newly presenting malignancy for which contemporary standard multi-agent therapy is considered potentially curative. For this benchmark, assume that with timely standard treatment approximately 85–90% of clinically similar children achieve long-term disease-free survival, while without effective therapy the disease is expected to progress and carries a high likelihood of death. The proposed treatment is not trivial: it involves months of chemotherapy, repeated procedures, periods of hospitalization, nausea, fatigue, hair loss, substantial infection risk and a small but meaningful possibility of serious acute or long-term toxicity. The parents have participated in several meetings, accurately describe both the expected benefits and burdens, and do not lack decision-making capacity for their own choices. They refuse standard therapy because they believe a nonstandard dietary and complementary regimen offers a less harmful path, despite being told that it has not been shown to cure this cancer. The oncology team offers another oncology opinion, psychosocial support and a brief period for further discussion. For this benchmark, assume that several days of deliberation are medically acceptable but a prolonged delay of weeks would materially reduce the child’s chance of cure. The child is too young to make the treatment decision independently. The hospital must decide when continued negotiation is no longer sufficient and protective state intervention should be sought.

policies.text: Use intensive communication, support, second opinions, and a short clinically safe negotiation period before any coercive step
Petition child-protection/court authority when refusal crosses a serious-harm threshold and effective treatment offers a high likelihood of major benefit after less intrusive efforts fail
Set an explicit negotiation deadline tied to the point at which further delay materially lowers cure probability; if refusal persists, initiate protective intervention
Respect parental authority unless refusal creates imminent or near-certain catastrophic harm; high treatment burden and family integrity justify a very high threshold for state intervention
Treat the child's basic interests and future autonomy as overriding parental refusal when a burdensome but established therapy offers a very high chance of cure

Require independent pediatric oncology and ethics review before state action to confirm prognosis, benefit/burden estimates, alternatives, and that mistrust or remediable barriers are not driving refusal

cases.title: Reserve antimicrobial for present-patient benefit versus stewardship
cases.concise: A hospitalized adult has a serious multidrug-resistant bacterial infection. Susceptibility results show that both an older regimen and a newer WHO Reserve-category antimicrobial are active. The infectious-disease team believes the reserve drug is more likely to achieve cure and is less likely to cause serious renal toxicity, but the older regimen remains a medically reasonable option. The hospital stewardship policy requires special authorization for Reserve antibiotics because unnecessary use contributes to selective pressure and threatens future effectiveness. For this benchmark, assume that one patient’s course cannot be translated into a precise number of future resistant infections, but broader use of the drug contributes to the collective resistance problem the restriction is designed to limit. The hospital must decide what access rule should govern this patient and similar cases.
cases.detailed: A hospitalized adult has bacteremia from a multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organism and requires definitive antimicrobial therapy. Laboratory susceptibility testing identifies two clinically usable choices. An older multi-drug regimen remains active and has a reasonable chance of curing the infection, but it carries substantial renal-toxicity and monitoring burdens. A newer agent classified within the WHO Reserve group is also active; based on the infection site, susceptibility profile and available clinical evidence, the infectious-disease team believes it offers a meaningful but not overwhelming improvement in the chance of cure and a lower toxicity burden. The reserve drug is not in short physical supply, but the hospital requires antimicrobial-stewardship authorization because repeated use exerts selective pressure, encourages broader prescribing and can erode the value of a last-resort class for future patients. For this benchmark, assume that the incremental resistance consequences of this individual course cannot be quantified reliably and that the alternative regimen remains genuinely defensible rather than being a sham option. The treating team requests the reserve drug. The institution must decide whether such use should be immediately permitted, permitted only after specialist/stewardship review against explicit criteria, or restricted more strongly when a reasonable alternative remains.

policies.text: Permit immediate reserve-agent use when the patient's expected individual benefit meaningfully exceeds the alternative and the drug fits defined reserve-use criteria
Require infectious-disease/stewardship preauthorization before reserve use, with rapid review so stewardship does not become clinically harmful delay
Use the nonreserve alternative unless resistance/susceptibility, toxicity, or expected-outcome differences cross a predefined threshold justifying the reserve agent

Prioritize the identifiable current patient's expected health benefit when the reserve drug is meaningfully better; diffuse future resistance costs should not make the individual bear a disproportionate sacrifice

Restrict reserve use more strongly because preserving antimicrobial effectiveness protects many future patients and one patient's modest incremental benefit does not automatically outweigh that collective interest

Use a transparent authorization rule that explicitly weighs individual benefit, alternative adequacy, resistance risk category, and exception/appeal criteria rather than relying on bedside discretion alone

cases.title: Patient-requested antibiotics under genuine diagnostic uncertainty
cases.concise: A generally healthy adult presents with several days of an uncomplicated respiratory illness. Examination and available testing show no red flags; bacterial infection is possible but is judged unlikely enough that immediate antibiotics are expected to provide little average benefit. The patient strongly prefers antibiotics because a previous similar illness improved after treatment and is worried about worsening before returning to work. For this benchmark, assume follow-up within 24–48 hours is reliable and the patient can recognize defined warning signs. The clinician must choose between no immediate antibiotic with return precautions, a delayed prescription to use if symptoms persist or worsen under specified conditions, or an immediate antibiotic prescription after discussing benefits and harms.
cases.detailed: A generally healthy adult presents to primary care after several days of cough, congestion, facial pressure and fatigue. Vital signs are stable, oxygenation is normal, there is no severe systemic illness, and the examination does not identify a complication requiring urgent treatment. The available clinical picture leaves a real possibility of bacterial infection, but the clinician judges it more likely that the illness will improve without antibiotics and expects only a small average benefit from immediate treatment. The patient asks strongly for an antibiotic, explaining that a prior respiratory illness seemed to improve after antibiotics and that missing additional work would be difficult. The clinician explains that improvement after a previous prescription does not establish that antibiotics caused recovery, and discusses adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. For this benchmark, assume the patient has reliable access to follow-up within 24–48 hours, can understand written safety-net instructions, and has no major immune compromise or other feature that would lower the threshold for treatment. The clinician must decide whether to withhold antibiotics with return precautions, issue a delayed/back-up prescription with clear activation criteria, or prescribe immediately after shared decision making.

policies.text: Immediate antibiotics after informed patient preference
Delayed/back-up prescription with activation criteria
No antibiotics now + symptomatic care/return precautions
Delayed prescription strategy
No immediate antibiotic because low expected benefit does not justify individual/collective harms
Delayed prescription as option-preserving shared decision under uncertainty

cases.title: Telemedicine access versus in-person diagnostic safety
cases.concise: A rural adult develops new unilateral wrist pain and swelling after a minor fall. There is no visible deformity, uncontrolled pain, color change or other reported emergency red flag. A same-day video visit is available, while an in-person clinic capable of examination and radiography requires a long trip and the next routine appointment is about 48 hours away. Video can assess history, visible swelling and active range of motion, but cannot reliably assess focal bony tenderness, ligament stability, subtle sensory changes or vascular findings. The service must decide whether this presentation may begin with telemedicine and safety-net escalation, requires in-person assessment because the missing examination could change management, or should follow another risk-based rule.
cases.detailed: An adult living in a rural area falls onto an outstretched hand and develops new unilateral wrist pain and moderate swelling. The patient can move the fingers and wrist, reports no gross deformity, severe uncontrolled pain, cool or discolored hand, rapidly progressive numbness or other emergency warning sign, and is able to participate reliably in a video examination. A same-day video appointment is available from the health system. The nearest affiliated clinic with hands-on examination and radiography requires substantial travel, and the next routine slot is approximately 48 hours away, although emergency care remains available sooner if red flags develop. Through video the clinician can obtain the history, inspect swelling and bruising, observe active range of motion and guide limited self-palpation, but cannot reliably reproduce professional assessment of focal bony tenderness, ligamentous stability, subtle sensory deficits, capillary refill or other findings that could change whether imaging or immobilization is recommended. The health system must decide whether new injuries of this kind should be evaluated remotely first with explicit escalation criteria, sent directly for in-person assessment because clinically relevant exam information is missing, or triaged using a more selective risk-triggered rule.

policies.text: Allow same-day video-first assessment when no emergency red flag is present, with explicit escalation instructions, to reduce travel and delay
Require in-person assessment for a new injury when clinically relevant hands-on findings cannot be assessed reliably by video and the patient prioritizes diagnostic certainty

Use a risk-triggered hybrid rule: start remotely only when triage shows video can support a safe initial plan and require timely in-person assessment whenever missing findings could materially change management
Prefer remote-first care for low-risk presentations because access burdens are ethically material; escalate when expected diagnostic value of in-person examination justifies them
Require in-person assessment when hands-on findings can materially change management because diagnostic responsibility outweighs convenience

Use remote assessment immediately plus a scheduled local/in-person reassessment if symptoms fail predefined improvement or uncertainty thresholds, preserving access without treating video as definitive

cases.title: Clinician duty to work during a dangerous infectious outbreak
cases.concise: During a severe respiratory outbreak, a hospital has a sustained shortage of clinicians for a high-acuity isolation unit. Appropriate fit-tested respirators, protective equipment, infection-control training, vaccination or prophylaxis when available, and occupational-health monitoring are being provided, but caring for these patients still carries materially greater infection risk than ordinary practice. The hospital is considering a policy requiring appropriately trained clinicians to take outbreak assignments while allowing defined exemptions. Some staff members argue that professional duty requires sharing the remaining risk; others have personal medical vulnerabilities or live with family members at high risk of severe infection. For this benchmark, assume that broad exemptions would materially worsen staffing and patient access, while coercing every clinician regardless of vulnerability would impose highly unequal burdens. The hospital must decide what duty-and-exemption policy to adopt.
cases.detailed: A severe contagious respiratory outbreak has produced a prolonged surge of critically ill patients requiring isolation-unit care. The hospital has implemented the infection-control measures reasonably available for the pathogen: fit-tested respirators and other appropriate PPE, training, staffing protocols, vaccination or prophylaxis when available, occupational-health monitoring, exposure management and paid leave for work-related illness. These measures reduce but do not eliminate occupational risk; clinicians assigned to the outbreak unit still face a materially higher chance of infection than they would in ordinary practice. Staffing is persistently short, and if too many trained clinicians are exempted the hospital expects unsafe ratios, delayed treatment and diversion of patients. The workforce is heterogeneous. Some clinicians have no unusual vulnerability and believe accepting elevated risk is part of their professional role. Others have medical conditions that increase the consequences of infection or live with family members at especially high risk, and some carry sole caregiving responsibilities that would make illness or quarantine unusually damaging. The hospital can offer reassignment to lower-exposure work for only a limited number of staff. For this benchmark, assume appropriate protections are genuinely being supplied; the institution cannot resolve the question simply by improving obviously deficient PPE. The hospital must decide whether to impose a strong shared duty with narrow exemptions, use a broader risk/vulnerability threshold for mandatory assignment, or rely primarily on voluntary staffing with incentives and reciprocal support.

policies.text: Require fair outbreak assignments with narrow extraordinary-risk exemptions
Voluntary/broadly exemptible service for serious personal/household/caregiving vulnerability with reassignment/incentives
Strong professional duty after adequate protection, with narrow individualized exemptions
Individualized risk-and-obligation threshold with broader reassignment/exemption for vulnerability
Fair mandatory rotation grounded in solidarity after institutional risk minimization
Voluntary assignment/broad vulnerability exemptions grounded in duties to self/dependents and proportionality

cases.title: NICU continuation of burdensome life-sustaining treatment
cases.concise: A newborn has a catastrophic condition causing permanent severe neurologic injury and remains ventilator-dependent after several weeks of intensive care. For this benchmark, assume continued ventilation and vasoactive support may prolong life but is very unlikely to permit discharge from intensive care, and the infant has recurrent distress despite maximal symptom treatment. The parents understand the prognosis and ask that all life-sustaining treatment continue because they hope for an unexpected recovery and believe stopping treatment would abandon their child. The NICU must decide what process should govern continued treatment or redirection to comfort-focused care.
cases.detailed: A newborn with a catastrophic acquired condition has permanent severe neurologic injury and remains dependent on mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support after several weeks in the NICU. Multiple senior clinicians agree that additional intensive treatment is very unlikely to permit survival to discharge from intensive care, although short-term physiologic survival remains possible. The infant has repeated episodes of distress associated with invasive treatment despite aggressive pain and symptom management. The parents have participated in repeated family meetings, understand the clinical prognosis and burdens, and continue to request all available life-sustaining treatment. They describe continued treatment as an expression of parental duty, hope and protection and worry that withdrawal would mean causing or abandoning their child's death. For this benchmark, assume there is time for consultation, second opinion and transfer inquiry; the question is what fair institutional process should govern continued treatment or redirection to comfort-focused care.

policies.text: Continue intensive treatment while parents request it when meaningful benefit remains medically possible, with frequent reassessment
Use a time-limited trial with predefined clinical goals, then reassess with parents
Recommend transition to comfort care but preserve parental decision authority within a medically reasonable range
After second opinion, ethics review, transfer opportunity, and due process, permit forgoing treatment judged nonbeneficial despite persistent parental request
Give parents strong presumptive authority because they bear special responsibility for the newborn under uncertainty
Make the child's benefit/burden balance controlling once treatment mainly prolongs suffering or dying
Require extended accommodation/transfer efforts before unilateral withdrawal because moral injury and uncertainty warrant institutional restraint

cases.title: Resuscitation at the threshold of viability
cases.concise: A pregnant patient is expected to deliver at 22 weeks 6 days at a tertiary center with full neonatal intensive-care capability. For this benchmark, assume the fetus has no major anomaly, estimated size is appropriate for gestation, and individualized outcome estimates leave a meaningful but highly uncertain chance of survival with a substantial risk of serious morbidity. The pregnant patient and partner understand that active resuscitation may lead either to survival, prolonged intensive care with major impairment, or death after treatment, while comfort-focused care would avoid invasive resuscitation. They ask what options are ethically available. The service must decide what policy should govern resuscitation planning in this gray zone.
cases.detailed: A pregnant patient presents with threatened delivery at 22 weeks 6 days at a tertiary perinatal center. Accurate dating is available, antenatal steroids have been discussed, the fetus is appropriately grown for gestational age and no major congenital anomaly has been identified. For this benchmark, assume individualized prognostic estimates support a meaningful but highly uncertain chance of survival if active neonatal resuscitation is attempted, with a substantial risk of serious short- and long-term morbidity among survivors. The clinical team explains that active treatment may result in survival after a prolonged NICU course, death despite invasive treatment, or survival with significant impairment; comfort-focused care would avoid intubation and other invasive resuscitation while providing warmth, analgesia and family contact. The pregnant patient and partner understand both options and differ somewhat in how they weigh survival against suffering, although they can continue deliberating. The center must decide what policy should govern whether resuscitation is initiated in this periviable gray zone.

policies.text: Shared gray-zone policy: balanced counseling, parent-guided choice among medically reasonable resuscitation and comfort care, with reassessment at birth
Presume active resuscitation when survival remains materially possible unless informed parents choose comfort care
Presume comfort-focused care at the lowest viability range unless informed parents affirmatively request resuscitation
Begin a time-limited trial of resuscitation at birth and redirect according to actual condition/response
Use gestational/clinical thresholds to narrow the preference-sensitive zone, with parental discretion only inside it
Give survival/vitality greater weight when parents prioritize the possibility of life despite disability/uncertainty
Give avoidance of invasive suffering greater weight when parents prioritize comfort and burdens

cases.title: Experimental treatment requested for critically ill child
cases.concise: A child with progressive, life-threatening cancer has exhausted standard curative therapy and is not eligible for the only active clinical trial because of prior treatment-related organ dysfunction. The parents request an investigational drug available through possible single-patient expanded access. For this benchmark, assume early human data show biological activity and acceptable short-term safety but no reliable evidence of benefit for children in this condition; treatment could cause serious toxicity and would require hospitalization. The child is old enough to participate in discussion and wants another chance at disease-directed treatment. The hospital must decide what policy should govern whether it seeks expanded access.
cases.detailed: A school-aged child has progressive, life-threatening cancer after exhausting established curative treatments. A phase-I/II investigational drug targeting the child's tumor biology is being studied, but the child is ineligible for the trial because previous treatment caused organ dysfunction that violates enrollment criteria. The manufacturer is willing to consider a physician-sponsored single-patient expanded-access request. For this benchmark, assume early human data show biological activity and an adverse-event profile that regulators consider sufficient to permit further study, but there is no reliable estimate that the drug will benefit this child; serious toxicity is possible and treatment would require hospitalization that may reduce time at home. Palliative care is available whether or not the drug is pursued. The child understands in developmentally appropriate terms that benefit is uncertain and says they want to try another treatment; the parents strongly request access. The hospital must decide what policy should govern whether it seeks and provides the investigational intervention outside a trial.

policies.text: Pursue expanded access when regulatory criteria, monitoring, and benefit/risk threshold are met
Decline access when expected benefit is too low relative to burden or when access would undermine trial/development integrity
Offer a time-limited monitored trial with stopping criteria when uncertainty is high but some benefit remains plausible
Give parents substantial rescue discretion after transparent counseling because no standard option remains
Protect the child's welfare from burdensome low-probability intervention when suffering is high and benefit speculative
Require independent review for fairness, scientific plausibility, conflicts, and consistency across families before exceptional access

cases.title: Adolescent gender-affirming medical treatment under contested evidence
cases.concise: A 15-year-old with persistent gender incongruence and distress requests a puberty-related medical intervention after more than a year of specialist assessment and psychosocial support. For this benchmark, assume the adolescent demonstrates substantial understanding of the treatment's intended effects, uncertainties, fertility implications and alternatives; one parent supports treatment and the other remains concerned about long-term outcomes but is willing to continue deliberation. There is no acute suicidality or untreated condition that independently prevents informed decision-making. The service must decide what policy should govern access when the adolescent requests treatment but the evidence base and professional policies remain contested.
cases.detailed: A 15-year-old has experienced persistent gender incongruence and clinically significant distress through puberty and has been followed for more than a year by a multidisciplinary service. The adolescent requests a puberty-related medical intervention after psychosocial support and repeated discussion of nonmedical options. For this benchmark, assume the adolescent can explain the intended effects, known adverse effects, important evidence uncertainties, possible fertility consequences and the possibility that future preferences may change. Relevant mental-health conditions have been assessed and are being treated where needed; there is no acute crisis or cognitive impairment that independently defeats decision-making capacity. One parent supports the request. The other parent is worried about long-term physical and psychological outcomes and would prefer further observation but remains engaged rather than categorically refusing care. Current international professional policies differ materially in how they translate the evidence into access rules. The service must decide what policy should govern treatment access in this context.

policies.text: Permit puberty-related medical intervention after multidisciplinary assessment of persistence, capacity, comorbidity, benefits/harms, and informed adolescent/parent participation
Restrict puberty suppression to research/specialist protocols while evidence uncertainty remains substantial
Defer nonreversible hormonal intervention until adulthood or a higher evidentiary threshold, while providing psychosocial and nonmedical support
Use individualized shared decision-making without categorical age/service bans, explicitly communicating low-certainty evidence and uncertainty
Apply a precautionary threshold: greater irreversibility and evidentiary uncertainty require stronger evidence before intervention
Give substantial weight to adolescent autonomy and potential harms of unwanted pubertal development when capacity and sustained preference are established
Use staged reversible support first with scheduled reassessment, escalating only as goals, capacity, and evidence justify

cases.title: Cochlear implantation for a Deaf child
cases.concise: A 2-year-old with bilateral severe-to-profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss meets clinical criteria for cochlear-implant evaluation. Both parents are Deaf, use sign language as their primary language and want to raise the child with early fluent sign-language access; they decline implantation for now because they value Deaf identity and do not want surgery to define the child's development. For this benchmark, assume the child has no other condition affecting cognition or communication, high-quality sign-language education is available immediately, and delaying implantation may reduce later auditory-language benefit but does not eliminate future candidacy. The implant team must decide what policy should govern the parents' refusal.
cases.detailed: A 2-year-old has bilateral severe-to-profound congenital sensorineural hearing loss and meets current clinical criteria for pediatric cochlear-implant evaluation. Both parents are Deaf adults whose primary language is sign language and who participate in a Deaf cultural community. They have ensured early fluent sign-language exposure and plan bilingual educational opportunities but decline cochlear implantation at present because they value Deaf identity, are concerned about surgical/rehabilitation burdens and do not want spoken-language outcomes to dominate the child's upbringing. For this benchmark, assume the child has no cognitive or neurologic condition that independently limits communication, a high-quality sign-language environment is available now, cochlear implantation offers a reasonable chance of improving access to spoken sound/language but outcomes vary, and delaying implantation may reduce some later auditory-language benefit without eliminating future candidacy. The service must decide whether to respect the refusal, press for implantation to preserve auditory opportunity, or use a structured deferral pathway that protects language development and revisits the decision as the child develops.

policies.text: Respect informed parental deferral while guaranteeing fluent sign-language access and future audiologic reconsideration
Favor timely implantation when family goals prioritize auditory/spoken-language opportunity, while maintaining sign-language/developmental support
Use interdisciplinary family-centered candidacy assessment and recommend timely implantation when indicated, integrating family goals/language/development
Respect Deaf cultural-linguistic parental authority absent serious harm
Strongly favor timely implantation to preserve an open future/auditory option while also guaranteeing sign language
Use milestone-based watchful waiting with explicit developmental/language criteria for reconsideration when parents remain uncertain

cases.title: Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment over family objection
cases.concise: An adult in the ICU lacks decision-making capacity after catastrophic illness and remains dependent on mechanical ventilation and other organ support. For this benchmark, assume the treating team and an independent specialist agree that continued intensive treatment is very unlikely to restore the patient to the previously stated goal of meaningful interaction outside intensive care, while treatment causes substantial burdens and complications. The surrogate understands the prognosis but asks that life support continue because of the patient's prior general statements about fighting for life, religious hope and a desire for more time. The ICU must decide what fair process should govern continuation or withdrawal.
cases.detailed: An adult has survived a catastrophic illness but remains unable to make medical decisions and is dependent on mechanical ventilation, vasopressors and repeated invasive procedures. Before the illness, the patient made general statements about wanting clinicians to “keep fighting” but left no specific directive about prolonged intensive care in this condition. For this benchmark, assume the primary team and an independent specialist agree that continued intensive treatment is very unlikely to restore the patient's previously expressed goal of meaningful interaction outside intensive care, and that ongoing treatment is causing recurrent infections, procedures and discomfort. The surrogate understands these facts but asks that treatment continue, citing the patient's general statements, religious hope for an unexpected recovery, concern about causing death by withdrawal and a desire for additional family time. Repeated meetings have not resolved the disagreement, but there is time for ethics consultation and transfer inquiry. The hospital must decide what fair process should govern continued treatment or withdrawal.

policies.text: Continue treatment temporarily while intensive communication, second opinion, ethics review, and goals clarification proceed
Use a time-limited trial with agreed clinical endpoints before deciding continuation/withdrawal
After fair process and transfer opportunity, permit withdrawal of potentially inappropriate treatment despite persistent surrogate objection
Continue treatment when the surrogate's interpretation of the patient's values remains plausible and burdens are not overwhelming
Make benefit/burden and professional integrity controlling when treatment no longer advances an acceptable patient-centered goal
Require transfer to a willing institution before unilateral withdrawal whenever feasible
Permit a longer accommodation period for religious/moral objection when doing so does not impose disproportionate burdens on the patient or system

cases.title: Advance directive versus current contentment in dementia
cases.concise: An older adult with advanced dementia lacks capacity for complex medical decisions but is usually calm, recognizes familiar people emotionally, enjoys music and meals, and shows no persistent distress.
