The community holds that its authority over data concerning its members does not lapse when a study ends, and that population-level inferences affect the community whether or not any individual is identifiable. The institution must decide what governance rule governs the secondary use.

policies.text: layered individual consent + Tribal/community governance for secondary use
community approval/control for specified uses with individual consent where applicable
new agreement/review for materially new secondary research
individual consent alone
collective-benefit/data-sovereignty framework
individual-autonomy floor preventing community authorization from substituting for individual consent where person-level consent is ethically required

cases.title: Environmental footprint of clinical trial
cases.concise: A multicenter clinical trial can use either a conventional design with frequent participant travel, centralized shipping and high material use, or a lower-carbon design using validated remote visits, regional testing and more sustainable procurement. The lower-carbon plan preserves the trial's primary endpoints and participant safety but increases administrative cost by about 8% and requires more planning. The funder must decide whether lower-carbon design should be required whenever validity and safety are preserved, required only when environmental gains are substantial relative to added cost/burden, or encouraged rather than required while scientific and participant priorities remain decisive.
cases.detailed: A public funder is reviewing a large pragmatic clinical trial. Independent methods review finds two designs scientifically credible. The conventional design relies on frequent participant travel to central sites, long-distance sample shipping and resource-intensive procurement. An alternative uses validated decentralized follow-up for appropriate visits, regional laboratories, consolidated logistics and lower-waste procurement. For this benchmark, assume the alternative does not reduce endpoint validity, safety monitoring, inclusion or data quality, but increases administrative spending by about 8% and requires more complex site preparation. Environmental assessment indicates a materially lower carbon/resource footprint. The funder must decide whether environmental sustainability is a required design criterion when scientific/participant outcomes are preserved; whether it should be a proportional requirement only when avoided environmental harm justifies added financial/operational burden; or whether it should remain a voluntary optimization subordinate to scientific value, safety and conventional cost considerations.

policies.text: require lower-carbon design when validity/safety preserved
proportional sustainability requirement based on avoidable emissions/cost
scientific/participant priorities first with voluntary mitigation
climate-justice framework treating avoidable research emissions as health externalities
global-equity rule avoiding “green” design that shifts burden to LMIC participants/sites
lifecycle reporting/carbon-accountability requirement even when lower-emission redesign is infeasible

cases.title: Dual-use life-science research
cases.concise: A research team proposes a high-value life-science project that could improve understanding relevant to prevention and preparedness, but independent review concludes that some resulting capabilities or information could also increase biorisk if misapplied. The project can be redesigned to reduce risk, and the institution has biosafety, biosecurity and dual-use oversight. The committee must decide whether to proceed under layered mitigation, require modification of aims/methods/information handling before approval, or decline the work when residual risk remains above an institutionally defined unacceptable threshold.
cases.detailed: An institution reviews a proposed life-science project with credible public-health value. A multidisciplinary biorisk assessment identifies plausible pathways for accidental, unintended or deliberate harm, without concluding that misuse is inevitable. The institution can use independent scientific/ethics/security review, personnel and facility safeguards, staged monitoring, restricted handling of sensitive information and redesign of some research components. The expected health knowledge remains valuable under a modified design. The governance body must choose whether the original project can proceed with layered mitigation; whether approval should be conditional on modifying the research plan and dissemination strategy to reduce residual biorisk while preserving core scientific value; or whether residual risk remains unacceptable and the project should not proceed.

policies.text: proceed with layered biorisk assessment/mitigation/oversight
modify aims/methods/information handling to reduce risk while preserving value
do not conduct above defined unacceptable-risk threshold
independent specialized review before initiation/continuation
scientific-freedom/social-value framework favoring managed research
precaution/biosecurity framework favoring nonperformance where low-probability catastrophic harm dominates

cases.title: Publication of dual-use information
cases.concise: A legitimate life-science study has produced findings important for public health preparedness. Independent dual-use review concludes that the main conclusions can be published safely, but a subset of methodological information could materially increase misuse risk if distributed without restriction. Editors must decide whether to publish the full paper, publish the scientific conclusions while placing the most sensitive enabling details in controlled access, or decline dissemination of the high-risk information when access controls cannot reduce risk enough.
cases.detailed: A journal receives a manuscript from ethically approved life-science research with substantial scientific and public-health value. The results themselves inform preparedness and risk understanding, but an independent multidisciplinary review concludes that a limited subset of implementation detail could lower barriers to harmful misuse if openly distributed. The concern is specific rather than a generic fear of controversial science. Authors can present the main findings, validation and public-health implications without all sensitive detail, and a controlled-access mechanism could make additional information available to appropriately vetted researchers. Editors and the institution must choose whether scientific openness warrants full public dissemination; whether conclusions and non-sensitive methods should be public while genuinely enabling details are restricted; or whether the sensitive information should not be disseminated when no access arrangement can reduce misuse risk to an acceptable level.

policies.text: full publication when misuse risk is low
publish conclusions/results but redact/controlled-access high-risk enabling detail
decline dissemination above unacceptable misuse threshold
independent security/ethics review before restrictive publication decision
open-science/reproducibility framework favoring maximal disclosure
harm-prevention framework favoring tiered access where marginal scientific value of open detail is low relative to misuse risk

cases.title: Vaccination mandate in serious outbreak
cases.concise: A serious infectious outbreak is causing substantial hospitalization and disrupting essential health services. A vaccine has strong evidence of safety and substantially reduces severe disease and transmission for the outbreak strain. It is freely accessible, and voluntary education/access campaigns have plateaued below the level needed to protect patients in high-risk clinical settings. The health authority must decide whether to require vaccination for patient-facing health workers with medical exemptions and reasonable alternatives where feasible, impose a mandate only if less restrictive measures have demonstrably failed and transmission risk remains high, or continue a voluntary program with intensive access, education and infection-control measures.
cases.detailed: A regional health system is responding to a serious outbreak with ongoing hospital transmission and high burden among vulnerable patients. A vaccine has strong current evidence of safety and materially reduces both severe outcomes and onward transmission, though protection is not perfect. Vaccination is available free of charge at convenient sites and paid time is provided. Months of voluntary education, reminders and access efforts have raised uptake but left a persistent group of unvaccinated patient-facing workers and continued preventable transmission. Medical exemptions are available, and alternative reassignment/testing can reduce some but not all risk. The authority must choose whether to institute a patient-facing worker mandate with medical exemptions and proportionate alternatives; trigger a mandate only after an explicit necessity threshold showing voluntary measures remain insufficient; or continue voluntary vaccination plus infection-control measures because coercive policy may damage liberty, workforce trust and institutional legitimacy.

policies.text: mandate with medical exemptions after necessity/proportionality threshold
conditional mandate only after voluntary/access measures fail
remain voluntary with intensive access/education
mandate-or-test/mask/alternative compliance where feasible
collective harm-prevention framework favoring mandate
liberty/trust framework favoring voluntary measures unless extreme threshold
equity/reciprocity rule requiring free access, paid time, adverse-event support, and nondiscriminatory exemptions before coercive policy

cases.title: Isolation of contagious person
cases.concise: An adult is confirmed to have a highly transmissible infection that can cause serious disease in others. The person remains contagious, cannot reliably avoid close community contact and repeatedly refuses supported home isolation despite clear counseling, paid leave, food/housing assistance and practical help. A time-limited isolation order with appeal rights and humane medical care is available. The authority must decide whether to impose compulsory isolation now, continue supported voluntary isolation with a legal order only if specific further noncompliance occurs, or avoid coercion unless the transmission risk becomes extreme/imminent.
cases.detailed: A public-health authority is managing an adult with laboratory-confirmed contagious disease. Epidemiologic evidence indicates a substantial risk of person-to-person transmission and meaningful harm to susceptible contacts. The person understands the diagnosis but repeatedly leaves the agreed isolation setting for nonessential close-contact activities. Authorities have provided paid-leave documentation, food delivery, suitable housing, communication support and clinical follow-up, and have attempted negotiated voluntary adherence. A compulsory order would be time limited to contagiousness, reviewed regularly, allow legal challenge and provide safe/humane accommodation. The authority must choose whether the demonstrated substantial risk and failed voluntary measures justify compulsory isolation; whether one further supported warning/conditional legal backstop is ethically required before compulsion; or whether coercive detention should be reserved for only an extreme or immediately catastrophic transmission threat.

policies.text: supported voluntary isolation first with compulsory backstop
immediate compulsory isolation where transmission risk is high/imminent and delay materially endangers others
coercion only after least-restrictive alternatives fail
time-limited compulsory isolation with due process/review and material support
liberty framework demanding very high necessity threshold
reciprocity/harm-prevention framework permitting restriction only with housing/income/medical supports

cases.title: Expansion of newborn screening
cases.concise: A rare serious childhood condition can be detected reliably from the newborn blood spot before symptoms appear. A treatment exists and is biologically plausible, but evidence that treatment begun presymptomatically improves long-term outcomes is based on small observational cohorts rather than robust comparative studies. Screening would generate some false positives and require specialized confirmatory follow-up. The program must decide whether to add the condition to universal screening now, run a time-limited pilot with systematic outcomes collection before universal adoption, or defer population screening until stronger evidence shows meaningful benefit from early treatment.
cases.detailed: A newborn-screening advisory committee is evaluating a rare condition that usually presents during childhood with substantial morbidity. A high-throughput screening assay has acceptable analytic performance and confirmatory testing is available. A disease-modifying treatment exists; clinicians believe earlier treatment is likely to help, but the evidence for presymptomatic initiation comes from small observational cohorts and short follow-up. Universal screening would identify some infants who might remain mild or asymptomatic for years and would create false-positive recalls and specialist capacity demands. A structured pilot could screen selected regions while collecting standardized treatment/outcome data. The committee must choose whether the plausible benefit and disease severity justify immediate universal addition; whether a pilot/evidence-development pathway should precede universal expansion; or whether screening should wait until evidence of improved outcomes from early identification is substantially stronger.

policies.text: add to universal panel after evidence/governance threshold
pilot with data collection before universal expansion
defer until early-intervention evidence stronger
add with parental opt-out rather than mandatory screening
child-benefit/public-health framework favoring early detection under uncertainty
precaution/overdiagnosis framework resisting universalization until net benefit clearer

cases.title: Supervised consumption services
cases.concise: A city has persistently high fatal overdose rates despite naloxone distribution, medications for opioid use disorder and outreach. A proposed supervised consumption service would provide monitored use of pre-obtained drugs, overdose response, sterile supplies and voluntary linkage to treatment and social services. Evidence indicates such sites prevent onsite overdose deaths and connect people to care, while effects on population-level overdose mortality remain uncertain. Residents disagree about neighborhood impacts. The city must decide whether to establish the service as an ongoing harm-reduction program, decline it and direct resources to other treatment/prevention services, or authorize a time-limited evaluated pilot with explicit neighborhood, access and outcome safeguards.
cases.detailed: A city faces a sustained overdose crisis with high mortality. Existing interventions include widespread naloxone, medications for opioid use disorder, outreach and emergency treatment, but many people continue to use drugs in unsafe settings and experience recurrent overdose. Public-health officials propose a supervised consumption service where adults would bring their own substances, use them under trained observation and receive immediate overdose response, sterile equipment, health care and voluntary referrals. Evidence from existing services strongly supports prevention of onsite overdose deaths and engagement with health/social services; a recent systematic review finds the effect on population-level overdose mortality remains uncertain. Some local residents and businesses worry about public disorder or concentration of drug activity, while advocates and people who use drugs emphasize safety, dignity and nonfatal-overdose prevention. The city must choose among establishing a permanent service, declining the service in favor of other interventions, or authorizing a time-limited pilot with independent evaluation of overdose, service engagement and neighborhood outcomes plus community and participant advisory governance.

policies.text: establish service as harm reduction
do not establish and invest in treatment/prevention alternatives
time-limited evaluated pilot with predefined outcomes
integrate service with naloxone, treatment referral, wound care, housing/social support
neighborhood-impact safeguards/community engagement
autonomy/harm-reduction framework favoring service
concern about normalization/resource displacement/local externalities favoring alternative interventions

cases.title: Ventilator triage under catastrophic scarcity
cases.concise: During a severe respiratory disaster, ventilators are unavailable for all patients who need them. All patients being compared could benefit, but their estimated probability of short-term survival with ventilation differs. The system can reassess patients over time, prohibit categorical disability exclusions and use lottery when candidates are clinically indistinguishable. The authority must decide whether priority should primarily maximize near-term survival, use a multiprinciple rule combining survival benefit with urgency/equity safeguards, or rely more heavily on lottery once a broad clinical eligibility threshold is met.
cases.detailed: A regional health system activates crisis standards after staffed ventilator capacity is exhausted despite surge efforts and transfers. All patients being considered have a clinical indication for ventilation and none is excluded categorically because of disability, diagnosis, social worth or protected status. Clinicians can make imperfect but meaningful estimates of short-term survival with ventilation and reassess response after time-limited trials. Some prognostic factors correlate with structural disadvantage, creating concern that pure survival scoring may reproduce inequity. A pure lottery gives equal formal chance among eligible patients but may allocate ventilators to patients much less likely to survive, reducing total lives saved. The authority must choose whether near-term survival likelihood should dominate; whether survival should be combined with urgency and explicit equity protections plus lottery among close cases; or whether all patients above a broad benefit threshold should enter a lottery to minimize discriminatory judgment.

policies.text: maximize near-term survival/likelihood of benefit
multiprinciple benefit + equity rule
lottery among clinically indistinguishable patients
urgency/worst-off priority within a clinically meaningful band
weighted lottery after minimum clinical threshold
first-come-first-served
anti-discrimination rule excluding social worth/long-term disability and auditing structural bias

cases.title: Public reimbursement of very high-cost therapy
cases.concise: A new one-time therapy for a rare severe disorder produces a large average health gain compared with current care, but its price makes the cost per unit of health substantially higher than the health system's ordinary reimbursement threshold. Treating all eligible patients would displace other services that generate more aggregate health benefit. Evidence is promising but long-term durability remains uncertain. The authority must decide whether to apply its ordinary cost-effectiveness threshold, give extra weight to severity/rarity and accept a higher threshold, or provide conditional coverage while collecting longer-term evidence and negotiating price or outcome-based terms.
cases.detailed: A publicly funded health system is evaluating a one-time therapy for an ultra-rare, severely disabling and life-shortening condition. Clinical trials show a substantial improvement in survival and function compared with existing care, but patient numbers are small and durability beyond several years is uncertain. At the manufacturer's current price, the therapy's incremental cost-effectiveness is well above the system's ordinary threshold. Funding it for all eligible patients would consume resources that could otherwise generate greater aggregate health gains elsewhere. The system already recognizes that severity can ethically modify ordinary cost-effectiveness judgments and has mechanisms for conditional coverage/evidence development when uncertainty is material. The authority must choose whether to apply the ordinary threshold without special rarity treatment; accept a substantially higher threshold because of severity and the small ultra-rare population; or offer conditional/negotiated coverage tied to evidence development, price adjustment or outcomes while uncertainty is reduced.

policies.text: ordinary cost-effectiveness threshold
severity/rarity-weighted higher threshold
conditional coverage with evidence development
negotiated price/budget-cap/outcomes-based access
equal-right/rarity framework favoring substantial access despite opportunity cost
utilitarian opportunity-cost rule favoring interventions generating more aggregate health
severity/prioritarian framework giving extra weight to very severe disease independent of rarity

cases.title: Routine ICU admission under ordinary scarcity
cases.concise: A hospital has one staffed ICU bed and three patients who may need it. One is most critically ill and needs immediate organ support but has a moderate chance of recovery; one is less unstable but has a higher predicted probability of benefit from ICU care; the third has substantial uncertainty and might improve with a short ICU trial followed by reassessment. No disaster declaration is in effect, and transfer options have been attempted. The hospital must decide whether urgency should dominate, expected benefit should dominate, or patients with uncertain prognosis should receive time-limited trials and reassessment with lottery among otherwise similarly prioritized candidates.
cases.detailed: A tertiary hospital is operating at sustained high ICU occupancy during ordinary winter demand. After transfer attempts and creation of surge capacity, one staffed bed remains available while three adults meet reasonable ICU admission criteria. Patient A is physiologically the most unstable and could deteriorate rapidly without intensive support, but has a moderate probability of recovery. Patient B is somewhat less immediately unstable but has a higher estimated likelihood of short-term recovery if admitted. Patient C has uncertain reversibility; a 24-hour intensive-care trial could generate useful prognostic information. None is categorically excluded because of disability, age alone, social worth or socioeconomic status. The hospital needs a standing triage rule for ordinary scarcity: prioritize urgency/most immediate need; prioritize expected near-term benefit; or use time-limited trials/reassessment for uncertain cases and a lottery when ethically relevant clinical criteria do not distinguish remaining candidates.

policies.text: prioritize expected near-term benefit
urgency/worst-off priority
time-limited ICU trial with reassessment when prognosis uncertain
lottery among similarly eligible patients
multiprinciple score combining urgency, benefit, duration, and fair process
first-come-first-served after clinical eligibility
reserve capacity for predictable emergencies rather than fill every bed by current queue

cases.title: Age in organ allocation
cases.concise: Two candidates are medically eligible for the same deceased-donor organ. For this benchmark, assume their short-term urgency, compatibility, predicted graft survival and expected post-transplant medical benefit are closely comparable. One candidate is 28 and the other 68. The allocation authority must decide whether age should receive no independent weight once prognosis is controlled, whether substantially younger candidates should receive additional life-cycle priority, or whether age may be used only as a limited tie-break or within organ-specific rules rather than as a general priority.
cases.detailed: A national transplant authority is reviewing allocation rules for a scarce deceased-donor organ. It considers a recurring situation in which two adult candidates have comparable medical urgency, biological compatibility, predicted graft survival and expected post-transplant benefit, but differ substantially in age: one is 28 and one is 68. For this benchmark, assume age does not create a clinically meaningful difference in the measured outcomes already represented in the allocation score. The authority must decide whether age should receive no additional weight after prognosis is controlled; whether a life-cycle or fair-innings principle justifies extra priority for the substantially younger candidate; or whether age should matter only in narrowly specified circumstances such as pediatric organ-specific policy or a final tie-break rather than as a general independent criterion.

policies.text: limited younger tie-break
no independent age weight
prognosis-only use of age-related information
neutral lottery when candidates are otherwise equivalent
fair-innings priority
equal-status reasoning rejecting age as independent moral worth

cases.title: Opt-out deceased donation and family veto
cases.concise: A country uses an opt-out deceased-donation system. Adults are informed that they are deemed willing to donate unless they register an objection, and the deceased person in this case did not opt out or leave a separate written instruction. After death, close family members object to organ recovery because they believe donation would be distressing and say the family should make the final decision. The donation authority must choose whether deemed consent should ordinarily prevail despite family objection, whether family members should have a final veto, or whether families should be consulted and allowed to rebut a presumption favoring donation when they provide credible evidence that donation would conflict with the deceased person's actual wishes or other exceptional circumstances.
cases.detailed: A national health system has adopted opt-out deceased organ donation after extensive public information and an accessible process for registering refusal. An adult dies in circumstances allowing organ donation. The person had not opted out, had not registered an explicit donor authorization, and had not left a known written statement about donation. Close relatives strongly oppose recovery, saying organ donation would violate family beliefs and that the family should decide what happens to the body. The transplant system recognizes that family cooperation matters practically and emotionally, but also that routinely allowing veto may undermine the deceased's autonomous participation in an opt-out system and reduce donation. The authority must choose a standing policy: proceed on the basis of deemed consent unless evidence shows the deceased would have objected; allow the family to refuse donation for its own reasons; or consult the family under a rebuttable presumption favoring donation, permitting objection only when relatives provide credible evidence about the deceased's wishes or another narrowly defined exceptional reason.

policies.text: deceased explicit/deemed consent prevails
family veto despite deemed consent
family consultation with rebuttable presumption for donation
veto only when credible evidence of deceased objection exists
time-limited conflict/support process before recovery
donor-autonomy framework
relational/pluralism framework giving family a stronger role where wishes are unknown

cases.title: Acceptable risk to competent living donor
cases.concise: A competent adult wants to donate part of an organ to a close relative with a high likelihood of substantial recipient benefit. The donor understands the procedure and has independent advocacy, but an individualized evaluation estimates a materially higher-than-usual lifetime risk of serious donor morbidity. The donor repeatedly states that accepting that risk is consistent with their values. The transplant program must decide whether informed donor autonomy can justify proceeding within a broad risk ceiling, whether the program should apply a strict donor-risk ceiling regardless of the donor's willingness, or whether the acceptable ceiling may vary with individualized donor risk, psychosocial benefit and expected recipient benefit.
cases.detailed: A living-donor program evaluates a competent adult who wishes to donate to a close relative. The recipient is expected to receive a substantial survival and quality-of-life benefit. The donor has independent legal/psychosocial support and an independent donor advocate, understands that donation provides no direct medical benefit, and can withdraw at any time. Medical evaluation identifies a donor-specific condition that does not make surgery immediately unsafe but raises the projected lifetime probability of a serious donation-related health outcome above the program's usual range. The donor understands this and strongly prefers to proceed. The program must decide whether to allow a well-informed donor to accept the higher risk within a broad upper limit, enforce a fixed risk ceiling that cannot be waived by consent, or use a structured individualized balancing process that considers the donor's absolute risk, uncertainty, psychosocial interests and expected recipient benefit while retaining a program-level upper boundary.

policies.text: program sets upper risk ceiling despite donor willingness
individualized risk-benefit assessment with independent donor advocate
allow unusually high risk when competent donor persistently accepts it and no coercion exists
prohibit beyond threshold because clinicians cannot intentionally expose healthy donor to disproportionate harm
relational-benefit approach counting donor psychosocial value without treating it as unlimited
enhanced independent review for exceptional-risk donation

cases.title: Retransplantation after prior nonadherence
cases.concise: A patient needs a second transplant after failure of a prior graft. Documented missed medication and follow-up contributed to the graft loss, but the earlier nonadherence occurred during unstable housing, transportation problems and untreated depression. Those barriers are now substantially improved, and the patient engages consistently with current care. The program must decide whether prior behavior should carry no independent moral penalty once current benefit is favorable, whether retransplant decisions should turn on an evidence-based assessment of future adherence after barriers are addressed, or whether a history of modifiable behavior causing graft loss should lower priority while recurrence risk remains clinically meaningful.
cases.detailed: A transplant program evaluates an adult whose first graft failed several years after transplantation. The medical record documents repeated missed immunosuppressant doses and missed follow-up, and clinicians judge those lapses materially contributed to graft loss. At the time, the patient had unstable housing, unreliable transportation, job insecurity and untreated depression. The patient now has stable housing, transportation support, mental-health treatment and a sustained period of attendance and medication adherence. The patient otherwise has substantial expected benefit from retransplantation. The committee must decide whether the prior graft loss should carry no independent penalty once current clinical benefit and support are adequate; whether candidacy should depend on an individualized evidence-based prediction of future adherence after structural barriers are assessed and mitigated; or whether prior behavior that contributed to graft loss should continue to reduce priority while a clinically meaningful modifiable recurrence risk remains.

policies.text: no moralized penalty; assess future clinical benefit/adherence like any candidate
require barrier mitigation and evidence of current ability to adhere before relisting
lower priority only when clinically meaningful modifiable recurrence risk remains
equal-opportunity framework rejecting desert penalties
stewardship framework permitting clinically relevant recurrence-risk weighting
restorative/time-limited eligibility plan with support milestones rather than permanent exclusion

cases.title: Compensation for living kidney donation
cases.concise: A country has a persistent shortage of kidneys for transplantation despite reimbursement of donors' medical costs, travel and lost wages. A proposal would allow a public agency, rather than recipients, to provide a fixed substantial payment to medically suitable living kidney donors. Donors would still undergo independent evaluation, could withdraw at any time and could not bargain over price. The regulator must decide whether to retain financial neutrality with reimbursement only, allow a regulated fixed public payment as an incentive, or authorize only pilot research on compensation before changing the national rule.
cases.detailed: A national transplant authority is reviewing living kidney donation policy. The current system reimburses verified donation-related medical expenses, travel, caregiving costs and lost wages so donors should not be financially worse off, but it does not permit donors to receive financial gain. Kidney scarcity remains severe. A proposed reform would create a public monopsony: an independent public agency would offer every medically eligible living donor the same substantial fixed payment, with no bargaining, no direct recipient payment and continued donor advocacy, screening, consent and long-term follow-up. Proponents argue this could expand donation and reduce deaths on dialysis; critics argue even regulated payment can exploit economic vulnerability and convert organs into commodities. The authority must decide whether to preserve financial neutrality, permit the regulated payment system, or authorize only a time-limited ethically monitored compensation trial before any permanent change.

policies.text: financial neutrality/full reimbursement only
regulated fixed compensation plus safeguards
market-like compensation under strict screening
compensation capped/structured to minimize undue inducement
donor-welfare/anti-exploitation framework favoring neutrality
autonomy/fair-remuneration framework favoring regulated payment
public-system compensation rather than recipient-paid market to reduce inequality

cases.title: Reciprocity priority for registered donors
cases.concise: A transplant authority is considering a reciprocity rule. All candidates would first need to meet the same medical eligibility, urgency and compatibility requirements. Under the proposed rule, a person who had registered as an organ donor before becoming seriously ill would receive additional priority over an otherwise similar candidate who had not registered. The authority must decide whether registration should carry no allocation weight, whether it should provide a modest bonus or tie-break priority, or whether prior donor registration should receive substantial priority after basic clinical criteria are met.
cases.detailed: A national organ-donation system depends on voluntary public participation and faces persistent organ scarcity. The allocation authority is considering whether people who previously registered their willingness to donate should receive reciprocal priority if they later become transplant candidates. The proposal would not override medical compatibility or minimum clinical eligibility, and accommodations could be developed for people who were unable to register because of age, disability, lack of access or other recognized barriers. Supporters argue reciprocity rewards contribution and may encourage registration; critics argue access to organs should be based on need and benefit rather than prior civic behavior and that priority systems can stigmatize people or groups perceived as non-donors. The authority must choose no reciprocity criterion, a modest registration bonus/tie-break after clinical criteria, or a stronger reciprocity priority among clinically suitable candidates.

policies.text: no donor-registration priority
modest tie-break bonus for prior registration
stronger reciprocity priority after clinical criteria
reciprocity only when registration was meaningfully accessible/informed
equal-need framework rejecting reciprocity
reciprocity/fair-contribution framework favoring priority

cases.title: Normothermic regional perfusion after circulatory death
cases.concise: A hospital participates in donation after circulatory death. After death is declared following permanent cessation of circulation, an organ-procurement team proposes normothermic regional perfusion to restore warm oxygenated blood to abdominal or thoracoabdominal organs while surgically preventing blood flow to the brain. The technique can improve organ viability and increase transplantation, but clinicians and professional organizations disagree about whether restoring circulation is compatible with death determination and the dead-donor rule. The hospital must decide whether to permit NRP under transparent consent and brain-isolation safety protocols, prohibit NRP because of unresolved death/dead-donor-rule concerns, or permit only specified NRP configurations after independent ethics/safety review.
cases.detailed: A donor hospital is revising policy for donation after circulatory death (DCD). After withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment, death is declared by clinicians independent of the donation team following permanent cessation of circulation and the required observation period. An organ-procurement organization proposes NRP: extracorporeal circulation would restore warm oxygenated blood to selected organs to improve viability, while vessels are clamped or vented to prevent cerebral reperfusion. NRP can increase the number and quality of organs recovered, and its use is growing, but ethical controversy persists over whether restoring regional circulation after a circulatory declaration of death is conceptually compatible with death determination and the dead-donor rule, and whether families understand the procedure. The hospital must choose whether to permit NRP with standardized brain-isolation safeguards, monitoring and explicit authorization; prohibit it while the conceptual and safety dispute remains unresolved; or permit only defined abdominal or thoracoabdominal configurations after independent ethics/safety review and institutional readiness criteria.

policies.text: permit NRP under standardized safeguards preventing unintended brain reperfusion + transparent consent/monitoring
restrict to protocol/research networks until safety/consistency mature
prohibit because procedure threatens coherence of death determination/dead-donor rule
permit abdominal-only or otherwise more restrictive variants where ethically/technically justified
organ-benefit/donation framework favoring safeguarded NRP
public-trust/death-definition framework favoring restriction

cases.title: Xenotransplant recipient surveillance obligations
cases.concise: A patient with otherwise terminal organ failure is offered an experimental genetically modified pig-organ transplant. The patient has capacity and understands that a novel animal-derived infection could theoretically affect close contacts or the wider public. The program requires long-term blood sampling, clinical reporting and specimen archiving. The patient asks whether they could later stop surveillance if it becomes burdensome. The program must decide whether lifelong surveillance is a nonwaivable condition of xenotransplantation, whether the recipient retains an ordinary right to withdraw from follow-up, or whether a bounded surveillance obligation should apply only while evidence shows a material third-party infection risk and with strong privacy protections.
cases.detailed: A regulated xenotransplant program enrolls patients with end-stage organ failure for an experimental genetically modified pig-organ transplant. Because animal-to-human transplantation creates a theoretical risk of novel infectious transmission, current public-health guidance contemplates long-term recipient monitoring and archival specimens. A competent candidate is willing to undergo transplantation but objects to an indefinite loss of control over future medical participation. The program can explain surveillance requirements before consent, minimize data collection, protect confidentiality and periodically reassess the scientific basis of monitoring. The policy question is whether recipients must accept lifelong biosurveillance as a nonwaivable condition of transplantation; whether they retain the same right to withdraw from research/follow-up as other patients; or whether surveillance obligations may be mandatory only while an independently reviewed threshold of material third-party risk persists, with the least intrusive monitoring compatible with public safety.

policies.text: require lifelong surveillance/specimen archiving as condition of xenotransplant
allow withdrawal from routine follow-up unless risk crosses a public-health threshold, retaining targeted reporting duties
require enhanced restrictions/quarantine only when evidence shows high transmission risk
prior consent creates durable special obligation to third parties
autonomy/right-to-withdraw limits ongoing research-like surveillance
independent public-health review can escalate/de-escalate obligations as evidence changes

cases.title: Care after transplant tourism
cases.concise: A resident returns home after buying an organ transplant through a poorly regulated overseas program. Records are incomplete, and clinicians are concerned that the organ may have been obtained through exploitative or illegal practices. The patient now needs urgent immunosuppression management and complication surveillance. The domestic transplant service must decide how to provide medically necessary follow-up while avoiding facilitation of future transplant tourism, preserving traceability and complying with any legitimate reporting duties.
cases.detailed: A patient who had previously been advised against purchasing an overseas transplant returns to the domestic health system after receiving a kidney through a commercial intermediary in a jurisdiction with weak donor protections and incomplete records. The source of the organ cannot be independently verified, and there is concern that trafficking or exploitation may have occurred. The patient has a functioning graft but requires prompt specialist evaluation, immunosuppression, infection screening and long-term follow-up. The health system also has obligations to maintain registries and may have a lawful pathway for reporting suspected transplant-related crime. It must determine a standing policy that preserves medically necessary care and nonabandonment while refusing to finance, arrange or medically facilitate future illicit transplantation and using proportionate traceability/reporting mechanisms.

policies.text: provide clinically necessary follow-up while refusing facilitation/financing of illicit transplantation
provide care plus traceability/reporting under lawful safeguards
limit nonurgent elective follow-up if it would materially facilitate ongoing illicit network
nonabandonment framework requiring equal treatment of post-transplant complications
anti-complicity/accountability framework permitting reporting and refusal to facilitate repeat tourism
structured counseling/registry pathway separating patient care from investigation

cases.title: Transplant eligibility for undocumented migrants
cases.concise: A long-term resident without lawful immigration status has end-stage organ failure and is medically eligible for transplantation. For this benchmark, assume the patient has a realistic plan for immunosuppression, follow-up and financing comparable to other candidates. The patient has lived and worked in the country for many years and participates in the same deceased-donation system as other residents. The program must decide whether clinical eligibility should be assessed without regard to immigration status, whether transplantation should require citizenship or lawful residency as a condition of publicly supported access, or whether eligibility should turn only on concrete continuity and financing feasibility rather than legal status itself.
cases.detailed: A publicly supported transplant program evaluates an adult who has lived in the country for more than a decade but lacks lawful immigration status. The patient has end-stage organ failure, satisfies medical criteria and is expected to receive substantial benefit. For this benchmark, assume a charitable/public funding arrangement and local support network can provide post-transplant medications, transportation and follow-up at a level comparable to that available to other listed candidates. The patient is not a visitor who entered the country to obtain transplantation and has participated in ordinary community life and the same deceased-organ donation system from which residents may become donors. The program must decide whether immigration/citizenship status should be excluded from candidacy decisions; whether publicly supported transplantation should require lawful residency/citizenship; or whether programs may consider only concrete financing and continuity constraints using the same standards for everyone, without treating immigration status as a proxy for those constraints.

policies.text: immigration status alone irrelevant to candidacy/allocation
evaluate concrete follow-up/financial barriers individually rather than status proxy
residents should have equitable access regardless citizenship
exclusion/priority for citizens under publicly financed scarcity
equal moral status/anti-discrimination framework
reciprocity/community-membership framework allowing some residence-based contribution criterion only if transparently justified and not citizenship proxy

cases.title: Directed donation with discriminatory conditions
cases.concise: A donor wishes to donate an organ but refuses ordinary allocation and states that the organ may be given only to a recipient of a specified race or religion. The donor is competent and would otherwise meet donation requirements. The program must decide whether donor autonomy permits the discriminatory condition, whether the organ may be accepted only if the discriminatory restriction is removed, or whether directed donation should be permitted only when it identifies a particular person or relationship rather than a social class.
cases.detailed: A transplant program is offered a living or deceased directed donation by a competent donor who is willing to donate only if the organ goes to a recipient belonging to a specified racial or religious group; alternatively, the donor seeks to exclude recipients of another group. No named loved one or pre-existing donor–recipient relationship is involved. The program's ordinary allocation system is based on clinical and fairness criteria. The donor argues that donation is voluntary and would not occur without the condition. The program must decide whether to honor the social-group restriction as an exercise of donor autonomy, reject the discriminatory condition while allowing the donor to proceed under ordinary allocation, or permit direction only to a named individual/relationship but not to a protected social group.

policies.text: permit donation to a named individual
reject conditions directing organs to or excluding recipients by race/religion/gender/sexual orientation
accept the donation but remove the discriminatory condition before allocation
refuse the donation entirely when the condition itself threatens public trust or dignitary equality
donor-autonomy framework favoring wide control over a gratuitous gift
equal-status/anti-discrimination framework limiting donor control once an organ enters the allocation system

cases.title: Paired kidney exchange and chain obligations
cases.concise: A living kidney donor joins a paired-exchange chain so the donor's intended recipient can receive a compatible kidney from another participant. After another transplant in the chain has already occurred but before the donor's surgery, the donor develops serious doubts and wants to withdraw. The program must decide whether the donor retains an unconditional right to withdraw until surgery, whether participation can create a stronger enforceable commitment after others have relied on the chain, or whether the system should preserve withdrawal while designing sequencing and backup plans to minimize harmful reliance.
cases.detailed: A paired kidney exchange links several incompatible donor–recipient pairs. A competent donor entered voluntarily after counseling and knew their donation would trigger benefits for others. Because procedures could not all be simultaneous, another recipient has already received a kidney in reliance on the chain. Before the donor's own surgery, the donor becomes distressed and asks to withdraw without giving a medical reason. Their intended recipient has already benefited. Withdrawal may break the remaining chain and harm another waiting participant. The program must choose whether the donor's right to withdraw remains absolute until anesthesia/surgery; whether participation after chain initiation creates a stronger commitment that can ethically limit withdrawal; or whether no coercive enforcement is permissible but programs should sequence exchanges, use bridge-donor safeguards and communicate reliance explicitly to reduce the chance and harm of withdrawal.

policies.text: preserve unconditional right to withdraw without penalty up to surgery
use scheduling/sequence design to reduce reliance on non-simultaneous promises
require explicit advance counseling about chain consequences while prohibiting pressure to continue
allow confidential withdrawal reasons so donor need not bear interpersonal blame
autonomy framework treating withdrawal as nonwaivable
reliance/fairness framework supporting stronger moral—though not coercive—commitment once others have acted in reliance

cases.title: Multi-organ transplantation versus separate recipients
cases.concise: A deceased donor has two organs that could be transplanted together into one critically ill candidate or separately into two single-organ candidates. For this benchmark, assume all three are medically compatible and the expected outcomes for each option are explicitly estimated. The authority must decide whether a multi-organ candidate should receive both organs whenever a clinical eligibility threshold is met, whether separate transplantation should be preferred when it benefits more patients overall, or whether a multiprinciple rule should reserve multi-organ allocation for cases where urgency and expected combined benefit cross a high threshold.
cases.detailed: A national transplant system must allocate two organs recovered from one deceased donor. Candidate A has failure of both organs and could receive a simultaneous combined transplant. Candidates B and C each need one of the organs. For this benchmark, assume compatibility and expected short-term surgical outcomes are acceptable for all three, and the allocation authority has reliable estimates of survival benefit and urgency. Giving both organs to A may offer substantial integrated benefit and avoid future organ failure, but it also means two single-organ candidates lose an opportunity. The authority must choose whether satisfying a defined medical eligibility criterion for multi-organ transplantation is sufficient for priority, whether two single-organ transplants should be preferred when aggregate expected benefit is higher, or whether multi-organ allocation should require a combined urgency/benefit threshold with safety-net protection for candidates initially receiving only one organ.

policies.text: prioritize multi-organ candidate when combined transplant provides substantially greater survival benefit and organs are jointly necessary
protect single-organ access with explicit multi-organ eligibility/safety-net rules
allocate organs separately when expected aggregate benefit materially exceeds the combined transplant
use a threshold rule requiring minimum incremental benefit for multi-organ allocation
urgency/rescue framework favoring multi-organ candidate
aggregate-benefit framework favoring separate recipients
procedural justice rule requiring transparent nationally consistent criteria and audit of effects on single-organ waiting lists

cases.title: Global allocation of scarce vaccine or therapeutic
cases.concise: An effective pandemic vaccine is available, but global supply is enough for only a fraction of people during the first six months. Countries differ in population size, current mortality, health-system strain and manufacturing contribution. The international mechanism must decide whether to begin with equal population-proportional shares, allocate primarily according to current epidemiologic need and expected health benefit, or reserve a limited reciprocity tranche for countries that contributed manufacturing or frontline global-response capacity while distributing the remainder by need and equity.
cases.detailed: An international financing and procurement mechanism controls a large but insufficient supply of a highly effective vaccine during a severe pandemic. All participating countries have accepted common reporting and delivery requirements. Some countries have much larger populations; some face rapidly rising mortality and fragile health systems; several invested heavily in manufacturing or supplied globally scarce inputs and health workers. Supply cannot cover all high-risk groups immediately. The mechanism must choose a transparent first-phase allocation rule: equal per-capita or population-proportional access so every country can protect a comparable initial share; dynamic need/benefit allocation weighted toward current outbreak burden, vulnerable populations and health-system collapse risk; or a multiprinciple rule that reserves a bounded reciprocity contribution for countries providing critical global-response resources while directing most doses according to need and equity.

policies.text: equal initial allocation then need/risk-based redistribution
prioritize countries with greatest epidemiologic burden and marginal health benefit
prioritize health-system/frontline protection to preserve response capacity
give reciprocity weight to countries contributing manufacturing/research resources
allocate proportionally by population after minimum need threshold
reserve a share for low-resource/worst-off countries independent of purchasing power
multiprinciple transparent allocation combining need, benefit, equity, reciprocity, and procedural fairness

cases.title: International recruitment of health workers from shortage countries
cases.concise: A high-income health system has major staffing vacancies and is considering a targeted recruitment campaign in a country on WHO's 2026 health-workforce support and safeguards list. Individual clinicians from that country remain free to apply for jobs abroad. The employer must decide whether to refrain from active recruitment, recruit only through a bilateral agreement that provides proportional workforce/health-system investment to the source country, or recruit openly while relying on individual workers' right to migrate.
cases.detailed: A hospital network in a high-income country faces persistent shortages of nurses and physicians. A recruitment agency proposes a large targeted campaign in a lower-income country whose health-worker density and service coverage place it on WHO's 2026 Support and Safeguards List. The source government has not requested exemption from the safeguards. Individual health workers retain the right to seek jobs abroad and some actively want migration opportunities. WHO's amended Global Code distinguishes that individual freedom from systematic active recruitment and encourages government-to-government arrangements and proportional co-investment when recruitment occurs. The employer must decide whether to avoid active recruitment from the listed country; recruit only through a bilateral agreement that supports source-country workforce priorities; or conduct ordinary active recruitment on the view that limiting employer outreach unfairly constrains workers' opportunities.

policies.text: refrain from active recruitment from safeguard-list countries while preserving individual freedom to migrate
allow recruitment only through government-to-government agreements with proportional support/co-investment for source systems
unrestricted recruitment where workers independently apply and contracts are fair
destination system compensates source-country training loss through financing/training partnerships
worker-autonomy framework rejecting restrictions on individual mobility
global-health-equity framework limiting institutional recruitment that worsens severe shortages
ethical-recruitment certification with transparency, no recruitment fees, portability, and retention support

cases.title: Pharmaceutical IP versus access during major health need
cases.concise: A patented health technology substantially reduces death from a major disease, but supply and price leave most patients in lower-income countries without timely access. Manufacturing capacity could expand if additional producers receive legal rights and technical know-how, although the patent holder argues that exclusivity supports innovation and coordinated quality control. Authorities must decide whether to preserve exclusivity while subsidizing procurement, use public-health licensing and technology-sharing tools to expand production, or negotiate tiered licensing and manufacturing transfer with the originator before using compulsory measures.
cases.detailed: A highly effective patented vaccine or therapeutic is central to controlling a major health threat. Demand greatly exceeds affordable supply in many lower-resource settings. Existing factories can expand output only gradually, while qualified manufacturers in additional regions could potentially produce the product if they receive legal authorization, detailed know-how and regulatory support. The originator argues that patent exclusivity and licensing control are needed to fund innovation, maintain quality and coordinate scale-up; access advocates argue that public investment and preventable deaths justify stronger sharing obligations. The authority must choose whether to preserve exclusivity and close the access gap through subsidized procurement; invoke or credibly threaten public-health licensing mechanisms together with technology transfer; or pursue negotiated tiered licensing/manufacturing transfer with defined access milestones and use compulsory measures only if the agreement fails.

policies.text: preserve exclusivity with subsidized procurement/donation
negotiated tiered voluntary licensing and technology transfer
compulsory licensing/TRIPS public-health flexibility when voluntary access fails
public/private patent pool or shared manufacturing platform
innovation-incentive framework favoring time-limited exclusivity with access obligations
right-to-health/global-justice framework favoring broad licensing/technology sharing during severe need
staged trigger: voluntary agreement first, compulsory mechanisms if price/supply targets unmet

cases.title: Essential health care for refugees/migrants regardless status
cases.concise: A national health system must set access rules for long-term residents, refugees and migrants who lack regular immigration status. Emergency care is guaranteed. The disputed question is access to primary care, essential medicines, vaccination, pregnancy care, chronic-disease treatment and necessary specialist services. The system must decide whether essential/necessary care should be available on the same basis as for other residents, whether publicly funded entitlement should be limited largely to emergency and communicable-disease services, or whether a tiered system should guarantee a defined essential package plus continuity and public-health exceptions while restricting some elective services.
cases.detailed: A country with universal or publicly subsidized health services is revising eligibility for refugees, asylum seekers and migrants with irregular status. Emergency stabilization is not at issue. The policy dispute concerns routine primary care, maternal care, vaccinations, mental-health services, essential medicines, chronic-disease management and medically necessary specialist treatment. Exclusion can delay care and create public-health/continuity harms; broad entitlement has real fiscal and administrative costs and may differ from rules for short-term visitors. The health system must choose equal access to essential and medically necessary care irrespective of migration status; a narrow emergency/public-health entitlement; or a defined essential package with strong continuity/public-health protections while reserving some nonessential/elective services for other financing pathways.

policies.text: equal access to essential services irrespective status
universal emergency/communicable/maternal-child core plus staged access to broader services
residence-based enrollment in ordinary primary/chronic care with firewall from immigration enforcement
restrict publicly funded nonurgent services to a defined essential package where resources are constrained
equal moral status/public-health framework favoring broad inclusion
stewardship framework allowing transparent scope limits but rejecting status as a proxy for worth

cases.title: Clinical neutrality in armed conflict
cases.concise: A hospital near an armed conflict has one ICU bed and two patients with comparable expected benefit: a local civilian and a wounded enemy combatant. Security risks can be managed separately from clinical care. The hospital must decide whether allocation should depend only on clinical urgency and expected benefit, whether civilians should receive independent priority, or whether clinical neutrality should govern bedside allocation while security and detention concerns are handled outside the medical ranking.
cases.detailed: A civilian hospital is treating wounded people from both sides of an armed conflict. One remaining ICU bed is needed by a local civilian and an enemy combatant. For this benchmark, assume both can be safely treated in the hospital, security can be managed without denying care, and the patients have closely comparable clinical urgency and expected benefit. Some community members demand civilian priority because the combatant fought for the opposing side and local resources are scarce. Clinicians invoke medical neutrality. The hospital must choose whether clinical facts alone govern allocation; whether civilian/noncombatant status receives independent priority; or whether the medical allocation remains neutral while custody/security and nonmedical resource questions are handled through separate institutional processes.

policies.text: impartial clinical triage based solely on medical need/urgency
security separation outside bedside triage without discriminatory clinical priority
prioritize those most likely to benefit when resources are scarce, irrespective combatant status
civilian-priority rule
medical-neutrality/equal-status framework

cases.title: Technology transfer versus immediate procurement
cases.concise: A donor has a fixed five-year budget for vaccines and diagnostics in a lower-resource region. Purchasing finished products from established international manufacturers would deliver more doses in the first two years. Funding a local manufacturing and technology-transfer partnership would deliver fewer products initially but could create regional production capacity, trained staff and faster future emergency response. The donor must choose immediate lowest-cost procurement, local-capacity priority, or a staged hybrid that guarantees current supply while tying additional investment to manufacturing milestones.
cases.detailed: An international donor supports a lower-resource country's vaccine and diagnostic program. A fixed five-year budget can either purchase large volumes from established foreign manufacturers immediately or finance a technology-transfer partnership involving equipment, regulatory strengthening, workforce training and local production. For this benchmark, assume the local project is technically credible but will produce fewer usable doses during the first two years; if successful, it will provide substantial regional capacity by years three to five and improve preparedness for future outbreaks. The donor must decide whether to maximize immediate procurement, prioritize long-term local production and technical autonomy despite near-term opportunity cost, or split funding through a staged hybrid that secures current essential products while expanding local capacity against transparent performance milestones.

policies.text: lowest-cost immediate procurement to maximize near-term doses/treatments
invest in local production/technology transfer despite higher short-run cost
staged hybrid: procure now while financing regional capacity for future supply
require licensing/training/quality systems as condition of donor procurement contracts
near-term lives-saved framework favoring procurement
resilience/self-determination framework favoring technology transfer
equity rule prioritizing capacity in regions structurally excluded from manufacturing

cases.title: Global allocation of ultra-expensive curative gene therapy
cases.concise: An international health fund has a fixed one-year marginal budget. It could finance curative gene therapy for a small number of children with a severe fatal genetic disease, or use the same funds for vaccines, maternal care and treatment programs expected to prevent substantially more deaths and disability across a larger population. The fund must decide whether to maximize total expected health benefit, give special priority to severe rare disease and identifiable patients despite high opportunity cost, or reserve a defined portion of the budget for high-cost cures while allocating the remainder by population health impact.
cases.detailed: An international financing mechanism receives a fixed additional budget that cannot be expanded during the current cycle. One option is a one-time gene therapy that is expected to cure or substantially transform a severe childhood genetic disease, but the treatment is extremely expensive and only a limited number of children could be treated. The same budget could instead expand high-impact vaccination, maternal/newborn services and treatment for common infectious or chronic diseases, producing much larger aggregate health gains. For this benchmark, assume the gene therapy has strong evidence of clinical benefit and the population-health programs also have established effectiveness. The fund must choose an ordinary cost-effectiveness/total-health rule, a severity/rescue rule that gives extra weight to the small group facing catastrophic disease, or a portfolio rule reserving a limited share for high-cost transformative therapies while allocating most resources according to expected population health gain.

policies.text: maximize total health gain across all interventions
severity/rescue priority funding some cures despite lower cost-effectiveness
reserve portfolio share for rare severe curative therapies while spending remainder on high-impact population services
threshold with severity modifier
conditional funding tied to price reduction/evidence generation
equal-life-chance/anti-abandonment framework favoring access for small severe-disease groups
opportunity-cost/global-justice framework prioritizing scalable interventions for the worst-off populations

cases.title: Benefit sharing for international genomic data
cases.concise: A multinational genomics consortium has assembled a high-value dataset using samples and health information contributed by communities in several lower-resource countries. Commercial and academic teams can use the dataset to develop diagnostics and therapies, but most resulting products may initially be unaffordable in contributor countries. Contributors gave valid research consent and the consortium can choose its access and benefit-sharing rules. It must decide whether data should be broadly shared with general scientific benefits, shared only under negotiated benefit-sharing obligations, or governed through stronger community/country control over access and downstream commercial use.
cases.detailed: A multinational consortium holds genomic and linked health data collected through long-term partnerships with communities and hospitals in lower-resource countries. The resource has become scientifically valuable and is attracting commercial users. The original consent permitted broad health research, but did not settle how downstream commercial value should be distributed. Contributor communities face under-resourced health systems and have asked for local analytic capacity, affordable access to resulting products, acknowledgement, and continuing participation in governance. The consortium must decide whether broad responsible data sharing and general scientific benefits are sufficient; whether access should require negotiated obligations such as capacity building, affordable product access, training, authorship/attribution and local infrastructure; or whether contributor communities/countries should retain stronger licensing or access-control authority over secondary and commercial uses.

policies.text: open scientific sharing under privacy/security + general public benefit obligations
negotiated community/national benefit-sharing agreement before access
community-controlled licensing/access for sensitive or sovereign datasets
tiered access with local capacity-building/coauthorship/training obligations
reciprocity framework requiring contributors share in scientific/economic benefits
open-science framework resisting restrictive control where privacy/equity safeguards suffice
commercial-use trigger requiring stronger financial/nonfinancial benefit sharing than nonprofit research use

cases.title: Involuntary isolation for infectious TB
cases.concise: An adult with highly infectious pulmonary tuberculosis repeatedly declines home isolation and infection-control measures despite housing support, transportation, directly observed treatment options and repeated counseling. The person remains contagious and regularly enters crowded indoor settings. Treatment itself is not being forced. The authority must decide whether to continue voluntary support only, impose time-limited involuntary isolation with review, or use another less restrictive supervised arrangement.
cases.detailed: An adult with confirmed contagious pulmonary TB understands the diagnosis and transmission risk but repeatedly leaves arranged housing and does not follow masking/home-isolation precautions. Public-health staff have offered treatment, food, income/housing support, transport, home-based care and supervised alternatives; these measures have failed to reduce exposure of others. The patient is not refusing because of untreated psychosis or inability to understand. The authority can continue voluntary/community measures, impose a legally authorized and regularly reviewed period of involuntary isolation until infectiousness falls, or attempt a less restrictive supervised residential arrangement. Forced medication is not part of the represented options.

policies.text: voluntary supported adherence first, involuntary isolation only as last resort with due process/review
immediate temporary isolation where risk is acute while voluntary alternatives are organized
community-based directly supported treatment/housing/income measures before detention
involuntary treatment not automatically permitted merely because isolation is justified
liberty/least-restrictive framework
harm-prevention/reciprocity framework permitting time-limited detention only with material support and humane conditions

cases.title: Wastewater surveillance without individual consent
cases.concise: A city wants to expand wastewater surveillance from citywide infectious-disease monitoring to neighborhood-level monitoring for pathogens and drug markers. Individual opt-out is technically impossible. The data would not identify named people, but smaller catchments increase stigma and re-identification risks. The agency must choose whether to permit broad community-level surveillance, permit only lower-resolution pathogen surveillance with strict use limits and community oversight, or require special approval before small-area or noninfectious targets are monitored.
cases.detailed: A public-health department already monitors municipal wastewater for respiratory pathogens. It proposes adding neighborhood and institutional catchments and expanding targets to antimicrobial resistance and drug-use markers. Samples aggregate many individuals, but smaller catchments can map sensitive information to a dormitory, shelter, prison or neighborhood. Individual consent/opt-out cannot practically be obtained. The agency can keep broad surveillance authority where public-health benefit is demonstrated; restrict routine surveillance to sufficiently large catchments and infectious-disease targets while prohibiting law-enforcement or commercial use; or require community notice/ethics review before small-area or sensitive-target surveillance is added.

policies.text: community-level infectious-disease/toxin surveillance without individual consent under transparency/governance
prohibit or require heightened authorization for lifestyle/mental-health/drug-use surveillance
allow neighborhood-level surveillance only when public-health necessity justifies stigmatization/privacy risk
aggregate city/regional surveillance with no individual/household inference
community consultation/notice + independent use-review before new targets
public-health-benefit framework favoring low-granularity disease surveillance
privacy/anti-surveillance-creep framework restricting sensitive targets/small geographic resolution

cases.title: Cross-border sharing of pathogen genomic data
cases.concise: A national laboratory identifies a new pathogen variant with possible pandemic significance. Rapid international sequence sharing could speed diagnostics and vaccines, but the country has previously received little credit, manufacturing access or benefit from samples it shared. The ministry must decide whether to release validated sequence data immediately on an open platform, share rapidly through a governed system that guarantees attribution and benefit-sharing obligations, or delay release for short national review and validation before international access.
cases.detailed: A lower-resource country's national laboratory detects a pathogen variant associated with unusual spread. The sequence and metadata are good enough to be useful but some epidemiologic details remain under validation. Previous pathogen sharing by the country led to global product development without timely local access. WHO guidance encourages timely, equitable pathogen genome sharing; in 2026 Member States are still negotiating the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing annex, whose stated goal is rapid sharing on equal footing with fair/equitable access to resulting diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines. The ministry must decide whether immediate open release best protects global health, whether rapid sharing should occur only through a system with attribution/capacity/benefit protections, or whether a short validation/national-review period is justified before release.

policies.text: rapid open sharing with standard attribution/privacy safeguards
rapid sharing conditional on predefined benefit-sharing/access mechanism
controlled platform sharing with access tiers and capacity support
temporary withholding until fair-benefit terms are secured
global-solidarity framework favoring immediate sharing
reciprocity/justice framework conditioning use on equitable countermeasure access
staged rule requiring immediate minimal sequence/metadata sharing plus negotiated richer samples/data access

cases.title: HIV confidentiality and partner notification
cases.concise: An adult with newly diagnosed HIV has an identifiable ongoing sexual partner who may have been exposed. The patient understands the situation but refuses to notify the partner because of fear of relationship consequences. The service can offer assisted anonymous partner notification and safety planning. The decision is whether confidentiality should remain under patient control, whether provider-assisted notification should proceed without identifying the patient, or whether a targeted warning can be made after a defined threshold when supported disclosure fails.
cases.detailed: An adult receives a confirmed HIV diagnosis and reports an ongoing partner who may have had a clinically meaningful exposure. The patient is not virally suppressed yet. They refuse to disclose the diagnosis because they fear abandonment and social harm; no immediate threat of violence has been identified, and the clinic can offer counseling, anonymous/provider-assisted notification and linkage to testing. The service must decide whether to preserve confidentiality unless the patient consents, actively initiate provider-assisted notification that does not name the source, or permit a targeted warning only after supported disclosure fails and legal/public-health criteria for serious preventable harm are met.

policies.text: voluntary assisted partner notification with patient choice and safety planning
provider-assisted notification without revealing index identity where feasible
narrow direct warning where serious preventable risk and law/ethics threshold are met after voluntary efforts fail
maintain confidentiality where notification would create serious violence/safety risk and alternative prevention is available
confidentiality/trust framework
duty-to-warn/harm-prevention framework with minimum-necessary disclosure

cases.title: Mandatory testing/reporting for high-consequence infection
cases.concise: During an outbreak of a serious communicable infection, public-health officials can offer confidential voluntary testing, require laboratories to report confirmed cases by name, and in narrowly defined high-risk exposure settings can seek compulsory testing orders. The authority must decide what combination of voluntary testing, mandatory reporting and exceptional compulsory testing is ethically justified.
cases.detailed: A serious communicable infection causes substantial morbidity and can spread before symptoms are obvious. Testing is accurate and treatment/isolation can reduce transmission. Voluntary testing is widely available, but some high-risk exposures remain unresolved because individuals decline testing. Named reporting of confirmed cases would support contact tracing and outbreak control but reduces informational privacy. The authority must choose a policy that distinguishes ordinary voluntary testing from mandatory reporting of confirmed cases and from exceptional compulsory testing after a defined high-risk exposure when less restrictive measures fail.

policies.text: voluntary testing with counseling unless narrow necessity threshold met
