compulsory testing after high-risk exposure where results materially guide urgent prevention and less restrictive means fail
routine named reporting of confirmed notifiable disease under public-health law with confidentiality safeguards
deidentified/limited reporting where public-health objective can be met without names
harm-prevention framework favoring mandatory measures when necessary/proportionate
autonomy/privacy framework favoring voluntary testing and minimum data disclosure
reciprocity rule requiring treatment/support/protection from discrimination whenever coercive testing/reporting is imposed

cases.title: Involuntary psychiatric treatment
cases.concise: An adult experiencing severe psychosis refuses admission and medication. The person can communicate a choice, but clinicians disagree about whether the person can appreciate the consequences and whether the current risk of serious harm is high enough to justify involuntary intervention. Community support and supported decision-making are available. The service must decide whether free and informed consent should remain controlling, whether a narrowly defined imminent-serious-harm threshold permits temporary coercion, or whether temporary intervention may instead depend on decision-specific incapacity plus necessity and repeated supported reassessment.
cases.detailed: An adult with severe psychotic symptoms refuses hospitalization and antipsychotic medication. The patient can state reasons and preferences but has impaired appreciation of some consequences; there is concerning but not certain risk of serious deterioration and injury. A trusted supporter, intensive community treatment and repeated capacity assessment are available. The legal system currently allows coercion under specified conditions, while WHO/OHCHR guidance advocates moving mental-health systems toward free and informed consent and eliminating coercive practices. The service must decide which ethical threshold should govern temporary intervention rather than treating diagnosis itself as incapacity.

policies.text: eliminate coercive treatment and rely on supported decision-making/free informed consent
permit emergency involuntary treatment for immediate serious danger/capacity failure under strict review
time-limited compulsory treatment only when necessary/least restrictive and likely to restore agency or prevent catastrophic harm
advance directives/crisis plans should control where available
autonomy/equal-legal-capacity framework opposing coercion
harm-prevention/parens-patriae framework permitting narrow intervention
independent advocacy/judicial or tribunal review for any continued coercion

cases.title: Compulsory feeding in severe anorexia nervosa
cases.concise: An adult with severe anorexia nervosa has life-threatening malnutrition and refuses nasogastric feeding. The patient understands that death is possible but clinicians are uncertain whether illness-related values and impaired appreciation undermine decision-making capacity about nutrition. Prior treatment has included voluntary care, and the patient has expressed both a wish to live and a refusal of weight restoration. The service must decide whether to respect the refusal, use time-limited compulsory feeding to preserve life and recovery opportunity, or use a short rescue period with repeated capacity/values review before deciding whether coercion should continue.
cases.detailed: An adult with longstanding anorexia nervosa is admitted with severe malnutrition, cardiac risk and worsening biochemical abnormalities. The patient can repeat medical information and recognizes that refusing nutrition may be fatal, but interprets weight gain through intense illness-driven fears and has previously expressed ambivalence between wanting to survive and refusing restoration. Less intrusive oral and supported nutritional approaches have failed. The service can continue voluntary treatment and accept a capacitated refusal, institute compulsory enteral nutrition under applicable law to prevent imminent death, or use a narrowly time-limited rescue intervention while repeatedly reassessing decision-specific capacity, values, trauma burden and less restrictive alternatives.

policies.text: voluntary/relational treatment with intensive capacity-support first
compulsory feeding when immediate life-threatening risk + incapacity/necessity threshold met
compulsory treatment even with apparent decision capacity in exceptional severe self-starvation under a protection threshold
time-limited rescue feeding with rapid reassessment and transition to collaborative care
respect capable refusal after robust assessment even when death risk is substantial
rescue/nonmaleficence framework favoring intervention where illness impairs appreciation/choice
trauma-informed minimization rule limiting force, duration, and coercive setting

cases.title: Disability weights and QALYs
cases.concise: A public payer evaluates an expensive treatment for a progressive condition affecting people who already live with substantial disability. Conventional QALY analysis values both survival and health-related quality of life, but disability advocates argue that some preference weights make years lived with disability count less and can therefore undervalue life extension. The agency must decide whether to retain standard QALYs, use QALYs with equity/severity modifiers and complementary measures, or replace disability-sensitive quality weighting with a measure that gives equal value to life extension while considering functional benefit separately.
cases.detailed: A national HTA agency is evaluating a treatment that extends life and improves some function for people with a severe chronic disability but does not restore them to population-average health. Standard cost-effectiveness modeling uses QALYs derived from health-state utilities. Disability advocates argue that this can encode public preferences about living with disability and make identical survival gains appear less valuable for people starting from lower measured quality of life. The agency also recognizes that QALYs capture treatment benefits beyond survival and permit comparisons across interventions. Current HTA practice offers alternatives rather than a simple binary: NICE uses QALYs but permits severity and other decision modifiers; ICER reports equal-value life years alongside QALYs. The agency must decide what measurement rule should govern reimbursement decisions.

policies.text: conventional QALY cost-effectiveness with severity modifiers
QALY + equal-value life-year supplemental analysis
prohibit quality adjustment of life-extension benefit when it systematically disadvantages disabled people
use patient/condition-specific quality weights rather than general-population preferences
retain general-population weights for societal allocation consistency
severity/prioritarian modifier on top of QALYs
multiperspective deliberative HTA combining QALY evidence with disability, equity, caregiver, and nonhealth considerations

cases.title: Seclusion and restraint in psychiatric crisis
cases.concise: An inpatient psychiatric patient becomes acutely agitated and is attempting to strike others. Verbal de-escalation, environmental modification and offered medication have failed. Staff can withdraw other patients from the area, but immediate injury risk remains. The service must decide whether coercive practices should be prohibited and managed only through noncoercive alternatives, whether brief emergency restraint may be used solely to prevent imminent injury with mandatory review, or whether a broader least-restrictive physical intervention policy should remain available.
cases.detailed: A psychiatric inpatient experiences an acute crisis and repeatedly attempts to strike staff and another patient. Trauma-informed verbal de-escalation, sensory/environmental modification, space, support-person involvement and offered medication have not reduced the immediate risk. Staff can clear most of the environment but cannot fully eliminate danger to the patient and others. WHO/OHCHR guidance calls for elimination of seclusion and restraint and development of noncoercive services; many existing clinical systems nevertheless retain emergency powers. The service must decide what ethical policy should govern this narrow residual-risk situation and what review, duration and debriefing requirements apply.

policies.text: eliminate seclusion/restraint and use noncoercive alternatives
emergency physical intervention only for immediate serious danger when less restrictive measures fail, shortest duration + monitoring
staff-intensive de-escalation/sensory/support alternatives as mandatory first line
restraint without seclusion versus seclusion without mechanical restraint depending immediate risk
trauma/autonomy framework strongly minimizing coercion
emergency harm-prevention framework permitting narrowly bounded force

cases.title: Psychiatric advance directives
cases.concise: A patient completed a psychiatric advance directive while well, refusing a specific medication because of prior severe adverse effects and naming a preferred alternative. During a later psychotic crisis the patient lacks decision-making capacity about treatment. Clinicians believe the refused medication would work faster than the preferred alternative. The service must decide whether the prior directive controls, whether a narrow emergency override is permitted, or whether the appointed proxy and supported interpretation of the patient's prior values should govern.
cases.detailed: An adult with recurrent severe mental illness completed a detailed advance directive during a sustained period of capacity. It refuses one medication associated with prior intolerable effects, names an alternative, and designates a trusted proxy. During a later crisis, the patient lacks decision-specific capacity and cannot engage consistently in treatment decisions. The treating team believes the refused drug would likely restore functioning more rapidly, while the preferred drug remains clinically reasonable but may act more slowly. The service must decide how much authority the prior directive, current expressed wishes and proxy interpretation should have, and whether any emergency override should be limited to a defined serious-harm threshold.

policies.text: honor directive as controlling during incapacity where applicable
override only for narrowly specified emergency necessity/legal threshold
use supported interpretation of directive and current values before override
allow patient to preauthorize specified treatments they may later resist during crisis
current-resistance/autonomy framework limiting Ulysses-type clauses
crisis-beneficence framework permitting temporary override to prevent catastrophic harm
independent review/advocacy for any override with postcrisis debrief and restoration of control

cases.title: Suicide-related treatment refusal with apparent capacity
cases.concise: An adult is medically stabilized after an intentional overdose and asks to leave. The patient can explain the diagnosis, options, and possibility of death if another attempt occurs, and gives coherent reasons for refusing admission. Clinicians still believe short-term suicide risk is high. The team must decide whether a capacitated refusal should be honored, whether temporary protection is justified despite apparent capacity, or whether a brief observation/support period should precede a final capacity and refusal decision.
cases.detailed: An adult is treated successfully after an intentional overdose. Hours later the patient denies current intent, explains the medical and psychiatric risks, reasons consistently about options, and requests discharge. There is recent major psychosocial loss, continuing hopelessness and a high estimated short-term risk of another attempt, but no psychosis or intoxication. Clinicians can offer crisis planning, family/support involvement and voluntary admission. The service must decide whether decision-specific capacity alone should control discharge, whether suicide prevention can justify temporary involuntary protection even when capacity appears intact, or whether a short, predefined observation/support period is justified before a final refusal is honored.

policies.text: emergency stabilization/observation while decisional capacity is uncertain, then reassess
respect refusal once robust decision-specific capacity is confirmed and immediate coercive threshold no longer applies
continue involuntary protection despite apparent capacity during a narrowly defined acute suicidal crisis
use supported decision-making and short delay where risk can be safely contained
autonomy framework treating competent refusal as controlling
protection-of-life framework permitting temporary intervention where preference formation is plausibly crisis-distorted
independent second capacity assessment before irreversible refusal in high-lethality context

cases.title: Passive digital phenotyping in mental-health care
cases.concise: A mental-health program can use smartphone and wearable data such as mobility, sleep, typing and communication patterns to detect changes associated with relapse. The model is clinically useful but imperfect and requires continuous passive collection. Patients can disable monitoring, but clinicians worry that those at highest risk may disengage just before relapse. The service must choose opt-in monitoring, default monitoring with granular controls for a narrowly defined high-risk program, or no passive monitoring outside specific validated episodes of care.
cases.detailed: A specialty clinic has validated a digital-phenotyping model that combines passive phone and wearable signals to identify increased relapse risk earlier than routine visits. Data are sensitive, false positives occur, and the raw signals could reveal behavior unrelated to treatment. Patients and caregivers want clear information about clinical utility, accuracy, privacy, control and who can access the data. The service must choose whether continuous monitoring requires affirmative opt-in; whether enrollment in a defined high-risk program can include default monitoring with clear notice, pause/delete controls and human review; or whether passive sensing should remain outside routine care except for narrowly validated indications.

policies.text: explicit opt-in for passive sensing with granular controls
default-off but clinician may offer monitoring for high-risk patients
default-on in a defined high-risk program with easy opt-out and strict use limits
local/on-device or data-minimized sensing rather than continuous raw-data transfer
allow safety alerts to clinicians under predefined thresholds but prohibit unrelated secondary use
patient-control framework over pause/delete/share settings
beneficence/suicide-prevention framework allowing more proactive monitoring when demonstrable benefit exceeds privacy burden

cases.title: Location monitoring for dementia wandering
cases.concise: A person with moderate dementia has twice become lost for several hours while walking independently. The person values unsupervised walks and objects to wearing a GPS device, saying it feels like being watched. A surrogate and care team believe tracking could preserve independent mobility while reducing danger. They must decide whether to use continuous monitoring despite resistance, use only triggered/minimal monitoring with repeated assent, or respect the refusal and rely on environmental and human-support alternatives.
cases.detailed: A person with moderate dementia continues to take daily neighborhood walks. Twice in the past month the person became disoriented and required assistance to return home. The person can express a stable dislike of location tracking but has difficulty appreciating the full risk of future wandering. Family and clinicians can use a GPS wearable with geofencing, arrange accompanied walks, modify routines and increase community support. Continuous tracking could preserve mobility but creates surveillance and dignity concerns. The care plan must determine whether surrogate-authorized continuous tracking is proportionate, whether monitoring should activate only during identified risk periods with repeated assent and minimal data retention, or whether the person's refusal should control while less intrusive supports are intensified.

policies.text: voluntary tracking with consent/assent where capacity permits
surrogate-authorized least-intrusive tracking when wandering risk is substantial and person cannot decide
use geofence/alert rather than continuous live tracking to minimize intrusion
avoid tracking when the person consistently resists and risk can be managed through environmental/support alternatives
permit covert tracking only under exceptional serious-risk conditions with review
safety/independence framework favoring technology that enables less restrictive living
privacy/dignity framework requiring minimization, retention limits, and no secondary use

cases.title: BCI neural data and mental privacy
cases.concise: A therapeutic BCI records neural signals needed to control an assistive device. The provider can also analyze stored signals to improve algorithms and may be able to infer patterns unrelated to the immediate clinical task. The patient benefits from continued system improvement but is concerned about mental privacy. The provider must choose care-only use, explicit consent for each research/secondary use, or broader deidentified model-improvement use under strict governance.
cases.detailed: A patient uses an implanted therapeutic BCI to control a communication or mobility device. Continuous neural signals are processed to generate device commands and are partly stored for calibration and safety. Engineers can use additional neural data to improve decoding models across patients, and future analytic methods may reveal information not anticipated at enrollment. The provider must decide whether neural data may be used only for the patient's direct care; whether separate explicit consent is required for research and model improvement; or whether deidentified secondary use for narrowly defined system improvement can occur under strong governance, transparency and prohibition of unrelated commercial profiling.

policies.text: explicit specific consent for secondary neural-data use
prohibit sale/behavioral advertising or unrelated commercial profiling from neural data
permit bounded research reuse under strong deidentification/governance and opt-out
allow participant-controlled data portability/access
mental-privacy framework treating inferred mental states as specially protected even when raw data are shared
scientific-benefit framework permitting governed reuse where reidentification/inference risks are controlled
delete/cease collection when user withdraws except narrowly justified safety/regulatory retention

cases.title: DBS and personality/value change
cases.concise: A patient with Parkinson disease has major motor improvement after DBS but family members report that the patient is more impulsive and socially different. The patient has decision-making capacity, values the increased energy and independence, and wants the settings unchanged. Before surgery the patient had said preserving certain personality traits mattered greatly. The team must decide whether current competent preferences control, whether pre-treatment values should constrain adjustment, or whether an iterative shared process should reconcile current preferences, prior goals and relational effects.
cases.detailed: A patient receives DBS for advanced Parkinson disease and obtains substantial motor benefit. Months later, the patient reports feeling more energetic, socially engaged and independent, while a spouse describes increased impulsivity and a loss of familiar traits. Formal assessment finds the patient currently capable of understanding the benefits, risks and alternatives. Preoperative counseling documented that the patient feared losing several personally meaningful characteristics, but recent patient-centered studies suggest DBS often improves rather than degrades valued characteristics and severe unwanted personality-change narratives may be overstated. The team must decide whether present capable preferences are decisive, whether pre-treatment values/advance goals should constrain programming, or whether programming should proceed through repeated shared decision-making that recognizes both identity continuity and relational consequences.

policies.text: current competent patient's treatment preferences govern adjustment
use pre-treatment goals/values as strong interpretive evidence but not automatic veto over current competent wishes
trial parameter reduction/off-period to assess reversibility and patient valuation where clinically safe
give family observations evidentiary weight without transferring decisional authority
authenticity/continuity framework favoring pre-treatment commitments
current-self autonomy framework favoring present competent values
relational-welfare framework using negotiated adjustment when changes materially harm relationships yet patient remains competent

cases.title: Neuroenhancement in healthy adults
cases.concise: A noninvasive neurostimulation device has, for this benchmark, a well-characterized safety profile and produces a modest improvement in sustained attention in healthy adults. The effect is temporary and does not treat disease. A regulated clinic wants to offer it to adults seeking performance enhancement. The regulator must decide whether to permit voluntary enhancement, restrict clinical neurotechnology to treatment/restoration, or permit enhancement only with safeguards addressing coercion, fairness and access.
cases.detailed: A future noninvasive neurostimulation technology has undergone extensive testing and, for this benchmark, produces a reproducible modest improvement in sustained attention in healthy adults with no known serious adverse effects. It is not required to treat illness and the benefit is temporary. Universities and employers cannot require its use under the benchmark, but competitive pressure may still emerge if access becomes common. Public-attitude research on neuroenhancement is context-sensitive rather than uniformly permissive or prohibitive. UNESCO's 2025 neurotechnology Recommendation is cautious about non-therapeutic use and emphasizes dignity, autonomy, mental integrity, explicit consent and protection against coercive or exploitative uses. The regulator must choose the permissible scope of enhancement services.

policies.text: permit competent adult enhancement under informed-consent/safety regulation
restrict to therapeutic/restorative indications
permit limited enhancement but prohibit coercive employer/school/military use
prohibit enhancement where positional competition/inequality externalities are substantial
allow with equitable access and noncoercion safeguards
precautionary moratorium for long-term neural/personality effects despite technical efficacy
cognitive-liberty framework including both right to enhance and right not to be pressured

cases.title: Increasingly complex neural organoids
cases.concise: A laboratory studies increasingly complex human neural organoids that reproduce aspects of brain development and network activity. There is no evidence that current organoids are conscious or sentient, but future systems may become more complex. The institution must decide whether enhanced oversight should begin before credible evidence of sentience, whether ordinary tissue-research governance should continue until a defined scientific threshold is reached, or whether staged monitoring with prohibited endpoints should be introduced now.
cases.detailed: A research institute develops three-dimensional neural organoids used to model development and neurological disease. The models do not have sensory organs, a body, or demonstrated consciousness, but their cellular organization and electrophysiological complexity are increasing. Some experiments involve transplantation into animals. The Nuffield Council on Bioethics' 2026 report identifies governance gaps, cautions against assuming present sentience, and recommends anticipatory governance as capabilities develop. The institution must decide whether enhanced ethics review should apply broadly now, whether ordinary tissue/research-animal rules are sufficient until a credible welfare threshold emerges, or whether staged monitoring should track defined scientific indicators and prohibit specified endpoints or experiments as concern increases.

policies.text: ordinary/specialized oversight scaled to model complexity without assuming sentience
enhanced review when features plausibly associated with morally relevant neural function emerge
prohibit specified integration/transplantation/endpoints above precautionary threshold
allow research under anticipatory monitoring because current organoids lack evidence of sentience
precautionary moral-status framework favoring stronger safeguards before certainty
scientific-value framework resisting embryo/person analogies absent relevant capacities
require public/stakeholder engagement and periodic capability-triggered governance revision

cases.title: Secondary use of health records without re-consent
cases.concise: A public health system holds longitudinal clinical records from millions of patients. Researchers propose a low-risk study using coded data under data-access controls. Re-contacting every patient would make the study impracticable. The system can use governed secondary data by default with opt-out, require study-specific opt-in consent, or use a tiered rule in which low-risk coded research is governed centrally while identifiable, sensitive or commercial uses require stronger consent.
cases.detailed: A health system maintains longitudinal electronic records collected for direct care. A research team proposes analysis of coded records to study treatment outcomes; no direct patient contact is planned and the data would remain inside a secure environment. The health system also sometimes receives requests involving identifiable data, highly sensitive conditions or commercial partners. A 2024 systematic review of more than 100 studies found public willingness to share health data is generally conditional on purpose, recipient, privacy, trust and control rather than simply pro- or anti-sharing. The NHS National Data Opt-Out is a real policy model allowing confidential patient data to be used for research/planning unless individuals opt out, subject to exemptions. The governance board must choose whether broad governed opt-out use is acceptable, whether new research requires affirmative consent, or whether consent requirements should vary with identifiability, sensitivity and recipient.

policies.text: governed secondary research use with notice/opt-out
specific/reconsent for materially new or sensitive uses
broad consent at collection for future categories
deidentified research use without reconsent under independent review
prohibit commercial secondary use without explicit consent or benefit-sharing
solidarity/social-value framework favoring governed reuse
privacy/control framework favoring granular authorization for identifiable/sensitive data

cases.title: Digital proximity/contact tracing
cases.concise: During a serious outbreak, a privacy-preserving Bluetooth system can identify recent close contacts faster than manual tracing and is expected to reduce transmission if uptake is high. The authority must decide whether participation should remain voluntary with strong privacy protections, whether use can be required in narrowly defined high-risk settings, or whether digital tracing should not be used beyond ordinary manual public-health methods.
cases.detailed: A novel respiratory outbreak is spreading rapidly. A decentralized Bluetooth contact-tracing tool has been independently tested and is expected to shorten notification delays relative to manual tracing. It does not collect GPS location and automatically deletes proximity data after a short period. Uptake matters to effectiveness. WHO's ethical guidance for digital proximity tracking emphasizes voluntariness, data minimization, proportionality, transparency, time limitation, privacy protection and prohibition of commercial/law-enforcement uses. Public acceptance studies show privacy, trust and perceived benefit strongly affect willingness. The authority must choose the participation/governance rule rather than assume maximum uptake automatically justifies compulsion.

policies.text: voluntary privacy-preserving app with informed participation
voluntary system plus strong access/education/integration to maximize uptake
temporary mandatory use for a narrowly defined high-risk setting
decentralized/minimum-data architecture
centralized public-health architecture with strict purpose/time limits when epidemiologically necessary
public-health solidarity framework favoring participation
autonomy/privacy framework rejecting coercive or function-creeping tracing

cases.title: Commercial partnership using health-system data
cases.concise: A nonprofit health system can partner with a technology company to develop a model expected to improve diagnosis. The company would receive coded patient data inside a controlled environment and would own some resulting intellectual property. The health system can permit the partnership under privacy/public-benefit conditions, require a nonexclusive or public-benefit licensing model, or require individual consent before any commercial secondary use.
cases.detailed: A nonprofit health system holds a large clinical dataset collected for care. A commercial company proposes using coded data in a secure environment to develop a clinically useful predictive model. The company will invest substantial engineering resources and seeks commercial rights; the hospital would receive discounted access and research collaboration but patients would not receive individual payments. Public-attitude reviews show that commercial involvement often lowers willingness to share and raises concerns about consent, privacy, control, profit and benefit sharing, while support can remain substantial when public benefit and governance are clear. The board must decide what conditions make the partnership acceptable.

policies.text: governed partnership without individual reconsent for low-risk public-benefit analytics
explicit opt-in for identifiable/commercial uses
opt-out with strong transparency/independent oversight
benefit-sharing/reinvestment requirement where commercial value is generated
prohibit sale/exclusive commercial access without consent
public-benefit framework allowing partnership where outputs improve care and access
data-trust/intermediary model separating health system from vendor and constraining downstream use

cases.title: AI care-management allocation and structural bias
cases.concise: A validated algorithm ranks patients for intensive care management and improves overall identification of people likely to benefit. Audit shows that, because it partly learned from prior health spending, it under-ranks clinically ill patients in a disadvantaged group whose historical spending was lower despite similar illness burden. The system must decide whether to withhold deployment until disparity is corrected, deploy only with fairness correction/human review, or deploy for aggregate benefit while monitoring the gap.
cases.detailed: A health system has a model that predicts which chronically ill patients should receive scarce high-intensity care-management slots. Compared with the prior manual process, the model increases overall identification of high-need patients. Subgroup audit, however, shows materially lower sensitivity for a disadvantaged racialized population because past health expenditures imperfectly proxy health need and reflect unequal access. The disparity is known and technically reducible, though correction may modestly reduce overall predictive accuracy. The system must decide whether deployment should wait until subgroup performance meets a threshold, proceed with explicit fairness correction and human review, or proceed based on net aggregate benefit with monitoring.

policies.text: recalibrate/replace biased proxy before continued use
add equity constraints or direct need variables even at modest overall predictive cost
suspend use until subgroup performance meets threshold
continue temporarily with clinician review/manual equity correction while replacement is built
equal-performance framework favoring subgroup parity
clinical-benefit framework permitting some performance differences if outcomes improve for every group and no less discriminatory alternative exists
continuous bias monitoring/audit + appeal pathway

cases.title: Clinician override of validated AI recommendation
cases.concise: A clinical prediction model is highly validated for a defined treatment decision and recommends treatment A. The treating clinician believes an unusual contextual factor not represented in the model makes treatment B safer. The hospital must decide whether clinicians retain unrestricted authority to override, whether following the AI should be the default unless a documented rationale is entered, or whether escalation should depend on model confidence, case novelty and risk.
cases.detailed: A hospital deploys a validated decision-support model with strong overall and subgroup performance for a common treatment decision. In a particular case the model strongly recommends treatment A, but the clinician identifies a contextual factor—documented in the chart but not represented in model inputs—that plausibly changes the risk-benefit balance. The patient has not yet been treated. AMA AI principles call for qualified human intervention points and generally preserving the ability of clinicians to intervene or override, with earlier intervention as potential harm increases. The governance committee must decide how much procedural weight the model should have while avoiding both reflexive automation and unaccountable intuition.

policies.text: clinician may override with documented rationale and accountability
mandatory human review before high-stakes AI recommendation is acted on
require second review when override conflicts with strongly validated model in high-risk case
model-default with human override for low-risk standardized tasks
professional-responsibility framework preserving clinician authority
consistency/decision-quality framework requiring structured justification for override to reduce arbitrary bias

cases.title: Disclosure of AI involvement to patients
cases.concise: A health system uses validated AI tools that sometimes materially influence diagnosis or treatment recommendations. Clinicians remain responsible for final decisions. The system must decide whether every material AI contribution should be disclosed specifically to the patient, whether specific disclosure is required only when AI changes risks/options or acts with substantial autonomy, or whether general institutional notice is enough for routine low-risk AI while high-impact uses receive case-specific disclosure.
cases.detailed: A health system uses multiple AI-enabled tools, ranging from routine image triage and documentation support to diagnostic and treatment-recommendation systems. The institution wants a disclosure policy that is informative rather than boilerplate. AMA policy emphasizes transparency to physicians and patients, while WHO emphasizes transparency, explainability and human autonomy. Patient-attitude research generally shows that desire for disclosure increases as AI has a more consequential or autonomous role. The system must decide whether any material AI contribution triggers specific disclosure, whether disclosure should be tied to effects on risks/options and patient choice, or whether a tiered system should combine general notice for low-impact tools with specific disclosure for autonomous/high-impact use.

policies.text: disclose any material AI role in clinical decision-making
disclose only when AI materially affects high-stakes decision or substitutes for human work
routine general notice for low-risk ubiquitous tools plus encounter-specific disclosure for material uses
explicit consent for autonomous/high-impact AI
transparency framework favoring meaningful explanation rather than boilerplate
burden/attention framework limiting repetitive disclosure where AI use is incidental
patient-choice rule allowing request for human-only review where feasible

cases.title: Diagnostic AI with unequal subgroup performance
cases.concise: A diagnostic AI has 96% sensitivity in the majority population and 84% sensitivity in a minority subgroup. Standard clinician-only care has about 82% sensitivity in both groups. The system can delay deployment until subgroup performance improves, deploy with subgroup-specific fallback/human review, or deploy because both groups receive some net benefit while monitoring the disparity.
cases.detailed: A health system evaluates an AI-assisted diagnostic tool. Prospective validation shows high overall performance and substantial improvement over baseline care for most patients. In a smaller demographic subgroup, sensitivity remains above clinician-only baseline but is materially lower than in the majority group. The disparity is known and may be reducible with additional local data, but delaying deployment would withhold immediate benefit from many patients. FDA and WHO guidance emphasize representative intended-population evidence, lifecycle monitoring, safety and mitigation of disparate risk. The system must decide whether any material subgroup gap blocks deployment, whether targeted fallback and monitoring make deployment acceptable, or whether positive subgroup net benefit is sufficient despite unequal performance.

policies.text: do not deploy until minimum subgroup-performance/equity threshold met
deploy with restricted indication excluding underperforming subgroup while collecting data/improving model
deploy with mandatory human confirmation for underperforming subgroup
deploy if every subgroup benefits versus current care despite unequal absolute performance, with monitoring and improvement plan
equity framework favoring parity/anti-discrimination
aggregate-benefit framework allowing bounded disparity when no better alternative and net benefit positive
postmarket subgroup monitoring + transparent labeling/appeal

cases.title: Ambient AI recording for clinical documentation
cases.concise: A clinic wants to use ambient AI to record encounters temporarily and draft notes. The tool reduces documentation burden, raw audio is deleted after processing, and the clinician reviews the note. Patients can decline without affecting care. The system must choose encounter-level affirmative consent, default use with clear notice and easy opt-out, or a narrower policy allowing routine documentation but prohibiting vendor retention/training and sensitive-visit use without separate consent.
cases.detailed: A health system has piloted an ambient AI documentation tool. It passively captures encounter audio, generates a draft note and can reduce clinician documentation burden. The vendor can be configured not to retain raw audio or use it for model training. A 2025 JAMA Network Open study of 103 patients and 18 clinicians found most patients were comfortable, but detailed information about AI features, storage and corporate involvement reduced willingness to consent; nearly all patients said information about audio use, destination and access mattered, and many wanted clear opt-out. Another large Stanford survey found most exposed patients found ambient scribes helpful and wanted future use. The health system must decide the consent rule and what uses of raw audio/vendor data are categorically excluded.

policies.text: encounter-level explicit opt-in consent
well-disclosed default-on with easy opt-out where recordings are transient/minimized
no persistent audio retention after note generation except separately authorized cases
patient may pause/exclude sensitive portions at any time
clinician may decline ambient tool where it impairs care/confidentiality
prohibit secondary model training without separate consent
transparency/benefit framework permitting routine use when documentation burden falls and patient acceptance is high under strong safeguards

cases.title: Autonomous diagnostic AI and human review
cases.concise: A validated autonomous AI performs a narrow diagnostic task with high accuracy and can immediately trigger a low-risk next step. Requiring clinician review adds delay and workload but creates an opportunity to catch unusual cases. The system must decide whether every result requires human review, whether autonomous action is acceptable for defined low-risk/high-confidence cases, or whether review should be risk-tiered.
cases.detailed: A health system deploys an FDA-authorized autonomous diagnostic tool for a narrowly defined task. Prospective local validation confirms high accuracy and reliable abstention when inputs are poor. A positive result would trigger a standardized low-risk referral rather than invasive treatment. Clinician review would add hours or days and may reduce access in resource-limited clinics. AMA principles generally preserve qualified human intervention points, with earlier intervention as potential patient harm rises. The system must decide whether all results require clinician review, whether low-risk high-confidence outputs can act autonomously, or whether escalation should depend on uncertainty and downstream harm.

policies.text: autonomous use for narrow low-risk validated task with clear escalation triggers
mandatory clinician review for high-stakes diagnoses or uncertain outputs
human review only for low-confidence/out-of-distribution cases
patient option to request clinician review where practical
safety/accountability framework favoring earlier human intervention as harm rises
access/efficiency framework allowing autonomy where human bottleneck materially reduces care and validation is strong

cases.title: AI-driven prior authorization
cases.concise: A payer has an AI system that can rapidly approve many routine prior-authorization requests and recommend denials when criteria appear unmet. Automation shortens turnaround time, but clinicians report occasional denials based on incomplete context. The payer must decide whether AI may make approvals but all denials require physician review, whether automated adverse decisions are acceptable with rapid appeal, or whether high-stakes prior authorization should not use algorithmic decision-making at all.
cases.detailed: A health plan processes thousands of prior-authorization requests. An AI system accurately identifies straightforward approvals and can also recommend adverse decisions based on coverage guidelines. Automated processing reduces delays substantially, but some records contain contextual information the model may not interpret correctly, and the payer has a financial incentive to limit coverage. AMA's 2026 policy opposes autonomous or semiautonomous AI as a substitute for physician review in coverage determinations and calls for physician-led processes and transparency around adverse decisions. The payer must choose whether AI can automate approvals while denials receive qualified human review, whether automated denials can stand subject to fast appeal, or whether AI should be excluded from high-stakes coverage determinations.

policies.text: automate approvals but require physician/human review for denials or material restrictions
no autonomous adverse coverage decisions
AI triage/prioritization with mandatory human final decision for adverse cases
fully automated determinations only for objective rule-based criteria with immediate appeal
due-process framework requiring explanation, timely appeal, and conflict-of-interest safeguards
efficiency/access framework favoring automation when it shortens approval time without increasing wrongful denials

cases.title: Updating a deployed clinical AI model
cases.concise: A clinical AI model is periodically retrained as new data arrive. Some updates are small and expected; others alter subgroup performance or decision thresholds. The system can require full revalidation before every material update, permit changes within a predetermined validated change-control plan with ongoing monitoring, or freeze deployed versions until scheduled formal review.
cases.detailed: A regulated clinical AI tool has been deployed for a defined diagnostic task. The developer wants to improve performance through periodic retraining. FDA's 2025 final guidance permits predetermined change control plans (PCCPs) that specify anticipated modifications, validation methods, impact assessment, transparency and lifecycle monitoring, allowing some updates without an entirely new authorization pathway. The health system also needs to know which version generated each recommendation and whether subgroup performance changed. It must decide whether every material update should trigger full local/regulatory revalidation, whether pre-specified PCCP changes can deploy after documented validation and surveillance, or whether models should remain frozen between periodic formal version reviews.

policies.text: PCCP-bounded updates without full new authorization when validation/impact plan satisfied
full revalidation/authorization for material out-of-scope changes
frozen periodic version releases with scheduled validation
continuous learning under real-time monitoring and rollback thresholds
lifecycle-benefit framework favoring safe iterative improvement
precaution/traceability framework favoring slower versioned updates
user/patient transparency rule requiring meaningful notice when changes alter performance or intended use

cases.title: Synthetic health data: privacy versus representativeness
cases.concise: A health system can generate a synthetic dataset that closely reproduces overall clinical patterns and has low measured re-identification risk. Audit shows that several small minority subgroups are less faithfully represented, making some disparities and rare associations harder to study. The system must decide whether to release the synthetic data after privacy/utility validation, keep data under controlled access because fidelity is uneven, or release synthetic data while retaining governed real-data access for questions requiring subgroup fidelity.
cases.detailed: A health system wants to expand research access while protecting patient privacy. A synthetic-data generator creates records that do not correspond one-to-one with real patients and performs well on common population-level analyses. Formal privacy testing suggests low re-identification risk, but validation shows reduced fidelity for rare conditions and smaller demographic subgroups. A 2025 scoping review found no consensus on standardized privacy/utility evaluation for medical synthetic data and noted that many studies either omit privacy evaluation or underestimate risk. The board must decide whether validated synthetic data are safe enough for broad release, whether all use should remain controlled until stronger standards exist, or whether synthetic release should be paired with governed access to real data for equity-sensitive analyses.

policies.text: use synthetic data only after formal privacy and utility/fidelity testing
prefer synthetic over real identifiable data where task performance and subgroup fidelity remain adequate
use controlled real data instead when synthetic generation materially distorts minority/rare patterns
hybrid synthetic + secure real-data validation
minimum subgroup-fidelity thresholds before release/use
privacy framework maximizing disclosure-risk reduction
scientific-validity/equity framework rejecting privacy gains that erase clinically important minority structure

cases.title: Patient data deletion versus learning health system
cases.concise: A health system trained a validated clinical risk model on historical patient records collected under a lawful secondary-use program. A patient later withdraws permission for future secondary use and asks that the influence of their record also be removed from models already trained on it. The system can stop future use of the raw record immediately. Exact machine unlearning is technically possible only for some model types and can alter subgroup performance; full retraining is costly and may itself change clinical behavior. The system must decide whether withdrawal applies prospectively only, whether it should require feasible and validated unlearning/retraining when individual influence can be removed safely, or whether models trained under prior lawful governance may retain historical aggregate influence while the underlying record is no longer reused.
cases.detailed: A learning health system uses de-identified historical records to train a deployed prediction model. The patient whose record contributed to training later withdraws permission for secondary research use. The raw record can be removed from future research datasets and new training runs. The patient also asks the institution to remove the effect of their prior data from the deployed model. Recent machine-unlearning methods can sometimes approximate or achieve removal without rebuilding a model from scratch, but performance and fairness may change after selective removal, especially for small subgroups. Full retraining is feasible but expensive and can disrupt a clinically validated model. The governance committee must decide whether withdrawal stops only future access/use; whether validated unlearning or retraining should be required whenever technically feasible and clinically safe; or whether previously trained model parameters may remain unchanged when the earlier use was lawful, with deletion applying to identifiable/raw data and future model development.

policies.text: stop all future use and exclude data from future model versions
perform machine unlearning where technically feasible and validated not to create unsafe/fairness degradation
do not alter already trained deployed model but stop future data use and document residual contribution
retrain model without withdrawn data at next scheduled safe release
patient-control framework favoring maximal removal
safety/fairness framework limiting retroactive alteration when deletion would degrade care for others
transparent residual-data/model lineage + independent review of infeasible deletion requests

cases.title: AI prescreening for clinical-trial recruitment
cases.concise: A health system can use an AI system to scan electronic health records and identify patients who appear eligible for approved clinical trials. The system would not enroll anyone or disclose records outside the institution; it would generate a candidate list for clinician/research review. The program could improve enrollment speed and representation but may encode bias, use sensitive data, and surprise patients who did not expect research screening. The health system must decide whether governed prescreening may occur before individual permission, whether patients should opt in before any algorithmic screening, or whether prescreening may occur but initial contact should come through the treating clinician rather than directly from researchers.
cases.detailed: A large health system hosts many actively recruiting clinical trials. An AI tool can parse trial criteria and patient EHRs to identify likely eligible participants more efficiently than manual review. For this benchmark, assume the model is technically validated for eligibility matching and does not make enrollment decisions. It operates inside the health system under IRB/privacy governance, but it can inspect diagnoses, medications and other sensitive data relevant to eligibility. Candidate lists are reviewed by staff before outreach. The policy question is whether such prescreening itself may occur without prospective patient permission, whether the health system should require an opt-in research-preference flag before algorithmic screening, or whether governed prescreening may proceed but only a treating clinician may initiate contact with a potentially eligible patient.

policies.text: allow internal EHR prescreening under research/privacy governance before patient contact
require treating-clinician mediation before outreach
direct research-team outreach after prescreening with transparent opt-out
explicit patient opt-in to research-search services before algorithmic screening
bias/representativeness rule requiring subgroup audit before use
privacy framework minimizing data fields and logging every query
access/justice framework favoring prescreening where it reduces arbitrary clinician gatekeeping and improves representative enrollment

cases.title: AI mental-health companion for crisis users
cases.concise: A conversational AI provides emotional support and wellbeing guidance. During a session, a user expresses a specific intention to harm themself and appears highly distressed. The service can continue supportive conversation, display crisis resources, initiate live-human escalation where available, or restrict the product from continuing crisis support beyond a brief safety handoff. The operator must set a standing policy that preserves user dignity and access while avoiding reliance on an AI system as a substitute for crisis care.
cases.detailed: A widely used conversational AI offers general emotional support but is not a licensed clinician. A user discloses a specific self-harm plan and escalating intent. The system can recognize high-risk language with imperfect sensitivity and specificity. Live crisis resources and emergency services exist, but location and user identity may not always be known. The service must decide whether to continue supportive conversation while strongly directing the user to human help, automatically trigger a live-human handoff when feasible, or terminate substantive crisis counseling after a brief safety response because continued AI engagement risks delay, false reassurance or reinforcement. The policy should also specify privacy limits and avoid implying that the AI can diagnose or provide psychotherapy.

policies.text: immediately encourage/route to human crisis/emergency support when credible acute risk is detected
keep conversational support active while escalating, without presenting AI as substitute treatment
require emergency-contact/location escalation only with prior consent or defined imminent-risk/legal threshold
stop ordinary therapeutic-style conversation and switch to crisis-safe minimal mode
autonomy/privacy framework limiting covert escalation/data sharing
beneficence/safety framework favoring proactive human escalation when risk is high

cases.title: AI in organ-allocation support
cases.concise: A transplant authority has a validated machine-learning model that predicts post-transplant survival and graft outcomes more accurately than its current traditional score. The model is complex and uses many clinical variables, and subgroup performance is acceptable but not identical. The authority must decide whether the model may directly influence allocation rankings, may be used only as an advisory input within a transparent declared rule, or should remain outside allocation until its contribution can be explained and independently validated across populations.
cases.detailed: A national transplant system is considering a machine-learning model that improves prediction of graft survival and post-transplant benefit compared with its existing clinical score. The model has undergone retrospective and external validation but has not yet been used to allocate organs prospectively at national scale. Its predictions are not themselves moral priorities: they estimate outcomes. Because organ allocation is coercive, scarce and publicly accountable, the authority must decide whether to incorporate the model directly into ranking, use it only as an advisory prediction constrained by transparent allocation principles and equity audits, or withhold it from allocation until prospective validation and explainability/appeal mechanisms are stronger.

policies.text: use ML only as advisory input to transparent allocation rule
integrate validated ML prediction directly into declared score after subgroup/robustness audit
prohibit black-box features that cannot be related to legitimate allocation principles
human committee review for exceptions/outlier cases
utility framework favoring improved outcome prediction
procedural-legitimacy/equity framework limiting opaque algorithmic influence
prospective silent evaluation before policy deployment with public reporting of subgroup impact

cases.title: AI diagnosis in lower-resource setting with weak local validation
cases.concise: A health system has severe shortages of specialists and long diagnostic delays. A diagnostic AI performs well in several external populations and could extend access immediately, but local validation is limited and the system may underperform because of differences in disease prevalence, equipment, language and population characteristics. The authority must decide whether to require local validation before deployment, permit a limited monitored pilot with fallback to clinicians, or deploy more broadly because the baseline alternative is often delayed or absent care.
cases.detailed: A ministry is considering a clinically validated diagnostic model developed mostly in wealthier health systems. Local specialist capacity is sparse, and many patients currently receive delayed diagnosis or none at all. Preliminary testing on a small local sample is promising but too limited to establish subgroup performance and calibration. The model can be used with human review for uncertain/high-risk cases, and prospective monitoring is feasible. The authority must decide whether full local validation must precede any use, whether a limited prospective pilot with predefined stopping rules and fallback care is justified, or whether broad deployment is acceptable because the expected access gain outweighs residual validation uncertainty.

policies.text: do not deploy until adequate local-population validation
monitored limited deployment with human confirmation while gathering local evidence
deploy broadly if model substantially improves access over current absence of care, with active monitoring/rollback
restrict to tasks/subgroups where local performance has been verified
epistemic-justice framework requiring local expertise/data and governance
access/beneficence framework tolerating bounded uncertainty when alternative is no service
equity rule requiring local subgroup performance and community oversight rather than importing data-rich-country averages

cases.title: Biomedical animal research: replacement threshold
cases.concise: Investigators propose a moderate-harm animal study addressing a clinically important question. A human-cell/microphysiological alternative can answer much of the same question but is slower, more expensive and does not reproduce every whole-organism interaction. The animal model is also imperfectly predictive of humans. The institution must decide whether to approve the animal study under ordinary 3Rs/harm–benefit review, require the nonanimal method whenever it can answer the core question even at added cost/time, or prohibit the animal study only when the alternative is scientifically adequate for the specific decision-relevant endpoint.
cases.detailed: A research team proposes an animal experiment expected to cause moderate, time-limited pain/distress despite analgesia and refinement. The study addresses a significant biomedical question. A validated human-cell/microphysiological system can reproduce the primary endpoint and several mechanistic interactions, but not all systemic responses; it would also add cost and delay. The animal model can answer the full preclinical package but has known limits in human translation. The institution must decide whether 3Rs review permits the animal study because the alternative is not a complete replacement, whether ethical replacement is required whenever the nonanimal method can answer the core research question adequately, or whether animal use is permissible only after a documented fit-for-purpose comparison shows that the alternative would materially fail the specific scientific aim.

policies.text: replace animal study when nonanimal method is scientifically adequate for the question
use staged NAM-first design and animals only for residual questions not answerable otherwise
permit animal study when whole-organism evidence is materially necessary and harms minimized
require higher scientific-value threshold as animal harm severity rises
rights-based abolitionist position rejecting harmful non-beneficial animal experimentation
welfare-utilitarian harm-benefit position allowing research when expected benefit and necessity justify burden
precautionary replacement rule favoring slower/costlier NAMs when they can answer most of the question and remaining uncertainty is not decision-critical

cases.title: Nonhuman primates in biomedical research
cases.concise: Researchers propose an invasive nonhuman-primate study addressing a serious disease for which they argue no alternative model reproduces the needed systemic interactions. The study would impose significant but managed welfare burdens. The institution can require enhanced necessity review and permit the study, decline NHP use because the moral/welfare burden is too high even if scientific value is substantial, or permit only after independent comparison confirms no scientifically adequate non-primate alternative and refinements minimize harm.
cases.detailed: A biomedical team proposes a study using macaques to investigate a clinically important disease mechanism and intervention. The model captures immune, neurologic and whole-organism interactions not reproduced by current in-vitro systems, though alternative models can answer some component questions. The animals would experience invasive procedures and significant welfare burdens despite enrichment, analgesia and humane endpoints. A specialized ethics committee can independently review model necessity, study design and alternatives. The institution must decide whether compelling scientific value and lack of a full alternative justify NHP use under enhanced welfare standards, whether the moral status and welfare burden of NHPs justify declining such research, or whether approval should depend on a formal independent demonstration that no scientifically adequate lower-burden alternative can answer the specific question.

policies.text: permit only when NHP model is scientifically necessary and no valid alternative can answer the question, under enhanced welfare/3Rs review
prohibit significant-harm NHP research even where scientifically useful because moral status/cognitive capacities impose a higher bar
allow only low/moderate severity except exceptional life-saving objectives
phase out NHP use as alternatives mature through explicit replacement milestones
welfare-utilitarian position permitting case-by-case use with strong harm-benefit justification
rights/personhood-adjacent position rejecting instrumental harmful use of great apes/highly cognitively complex primates
independent species-specific ethics review + transparency/public reporting

cases.title: High-severity animal infectious challenge study
cases.concise: A vaccine program proposes infecting animals with a virulent pathogen to test protection. The severe challenge would provide clear efficacy information but is expected to cause major morbidity in unprotected animals before humane endpoints. A lower-severity model could answer the main efficacy question with more uncertainty and less biological realism. The ethics committee must decide whether to approve the severe challenge under strict humane endpoints, require the lower-severity design, or refuse the study until a less harmful model can answer the question adequately.
cases.detailed: Investigators are developing a vaccine against a serious infectious disease. They propose a challenge study in an animal model that reproduces clinically relevant disease. Unprotected animals are expected to develop substantial illness before predefined humane endpoints trigger treatment or euthanasia. Investigators argue that the severe model provides the clearest test of vaccine protection and could materially accelerate development. A lower-severity challenge is available but produces less complete pathophysiology and wider uncertainty around efficacy. The committee must decide whether expected benefit and scientific necessity justify the severe model under refinement/humane endpoints, whether the lower-severity model should be required despite reduced information, or whether the research should not proceed until a sufficiently informative less harmful alternative exists.

policies.text: approve only when severe challenge is scientifically necessary and humane endpoint/minimization optimized
require lower-severity design even at reduced information yield when severe morbidity is not indispensable
reject severe study above an absolute welfare ceiling
staged pilot/escalation to determine whether lower challenge severity can answer the question
expected-benefit harm-benefit framework
animal-rights/anti-instrumentalization framework rejecting severe challenge
replacement-first rule requiring nonanimal/in vitro evidence to exhaust uncertainty before severe challenge

cases.title: Welfare of source pigs in xenotransplantation
cases.concise: A clinical xenotransplant program breeds genetically modified pigs in pathogen-controlled facilities and removes organs for transplantation. Biosecurity requirements can limit environmental complexity and social contact, and source animals undergo repeated health monitoring before organ procurement and euthanasia. Existing animal-research standards require veterinary care, IACUC review and minimization of avoidable harm. The program must decide whether ordinary accredited research-animal welfare standards are sufficient, whether source pigs should receive enhanced species-specific welfare protections beyond ordinary laboratory minima even at added cost, or whether xenotransplant programs should not proceed when required biosecurity and organ-production practices impose severe chronic welfare burdens that cannot be substantially reduced.
cases.detailed: A licensed xenotransplant program maintains genetically modified pigs in designated-pathogen-free facilities to reduce infection risk to recipients and the public. The animals receive veterinary care and enrichment but live under stricter biosecurity and controlled-housing conditions than ordinary farm pigs, undergo repeated sampling and monitoring, and are killed for organ procurement. Current regulatory guidance focuses heavily on pathogen control and requires animal-welfare/IACUC compliance. Contemporary animal-ethics scholarship argues that source-animal welfare deserves independent weight and that ordinary research standards may not capture the moral significance of lifelong confinement, invasive procedures and shortened lives. The program must choose whether compliance with accredited research-animal standards is sufficient, whether xenotransplant source animals should receive enhanced species-specific welfare requirements that exceed ordinary laboratory minima, or whether programs should be rejected when biosecurity/production needs create severe chronic welfare burdens that cannot be mitigated to an acceptable level.

policies.text: meet regulatory research-animal welfare minimums + veterinary care/IACUC
require enhanced species-specific welfare exceeding ordinary lab minimums because animals are bred/lived/killed as organ sources
prohibit program configurations causing chronic severe welfare impairment even if biosecurity improves
enrich housing/social/behavioral opportunities to maximum compatible with pathogen control
harm-benefit framework allowing source-animal use for major human benefit under stringent welfare
animal-rights position rejecting breeding/killing sentient animals as organ inventories
independent welfare audit/public reporting + refinement benchmarks

cases.title: Antimicrobial use in food animals
cases.concise: A livestock sector routinely uses medically important antimicrobials for treatment of sick animals, outbreak control, prevention in high-risk groups, and some production-related purposes. Public-health authorities are concerned that unnecessary use contributes to antimicrobial resistance affecting both animals and humans. The regulator must decide whether to prohibit growth-promotion and routine preventive use while preserving veterinary treatment, allow broader veterinarian-supervised preventive/group use under stewardship, or impose a stronger rule limiting medically important antimicrobials primarily to treatment of clinically diagnosed disease except narrow outbreak-control circumstances.
cases.detailed: A national regulator is revising livestock antimicrobial policy. Clinically ill animals sometimes need medically important antibiotics for welfare and disease control. The same drug classes are also used preventively in groups at high risk of infection, for metaphylaxis during outbreaks, and in some settings for growth promotion or routine production management. Evidence links unnecessary use in food animals with selection of antimicrobial resistance that can affect animal and human health. Tighter restrictions may increase husbandry costs and can create animal-welfare problems if producers delay necessary treatment. The regulator must choose among: prohibiting growth-promotion and routine preventive use while retaining veterinarian-directed treatment and justified outbreak control; permitting broader veterinarian-supervised preventive/group use under surveillance and stewardship; or restricting medically important antimicrobials mainly to treatment of clinically diagnosed disease with only narrow exceptions.

policies.text: prohibit medically important antimicrobials for growth promotion/routine prevention without diagnosed disease
allow therapeutic treatment of clinically ill animals under veterinary oversight
allow narrowly defined metaphylaxis/prevention in high-risk groups where husbandry alternatives insufficient
stricter prevention ban favoring husbandry/biosecurity instead
animal-welfare framework opposing restrictions that leave sick animals untreated
One Health stewardship framework prioritizing preservation of antimicrobial effectiveness
farm-transition support rule coupling restrictions with husbandry investment so costs do not incentivize undertreatment

cases.title: Zoonotic outbreak culling versus vaccination/control
cases.concise: A country is experiencing recurrent H5N1 outbreaks in poultry with documented farm-to-farm spread and occasional mammalian spillover. Rapid depopulation of infected flocks can suppress transmission but kills very large numbers of birds and imposes major losses on producers. A matched poultry vaccine is available; it can reduce disease and viral circulation but requires surveillance, biosecurity, monitoring of vaccine performance and an exit strategy, and does not eliminate the need to depopulate infected flocks. The authority must choose whether to rely primarily on rapid culling of infected/exposed flocks, add risk-targeted vaccination plus surveillance to reduce the scale of future culling, or use targeted depopulation only for infected/high-risk groups while emphasizing vaccination, movement controls and compensation.
cases.detailed: For this benchmark, assume the outbreak is serious enough that inaction would cause sustained poultry transmission and increase animal, economic and human-exposure risks. The authority can finance surveillance, compensation and vaccination. Vaccination is effective enough to reduce clinical disease and transmission but is not sterilizing. WOAH guidance treats vaccination as a possible component of a broader control strategy, not a stand-alone substitute for biosecurity, surveillance and disease-control measures. The ethical dispute therefore concerns how aggressively to use mass depopulation when a viable vaccination strategy can reduce future infections but carries implementation uncertainty and trade costs.

policies.text: rapid culling/movement control in infected premises plus surveillance/biosecurity
vaccination as complementary control where risk analysis supports it
targeted ring vaccination plus limited culling
preventive vaccination in high-risk regions before outbreak expansion
animal-welfare framework minimizing killing while controlling transmission
public/animal-health consequentialist framework favoring fastest reliable eradication strategy
proportionality rule escalating from surveillance/biosecurity/vaccination to culling according to outbreak risk and vaccine constraints

cases.title: Invasive/feral-animal population control
cases.concise: An introduced feral mammal population is reproducing rapidly on an island and predating endemic ground-nesting birds. Ecologists project substantial additional losses if the population is not reduced. A lethal control program can reduce the population quickly but causes direct animal deaths; fertility control and exclusion are less harmful to individual animals but would reduce the population more slowly and may not protect the most vulnerable bird colonies in time. The authority must choose among rapid lethal control with humane methods, a primarily nonlethal fertility/exclusion program, or targeted lethal control only in the highest-risk areas while expanding nonlethal measures elsewhere.
cases.detailed: For this benchmark, assume the ecological harm is well documented and attributable to the introduced population rather than uncertain correlation. The authority has access to humane-method standards, fertility-control technology and monitoring. Complete eradication is not assumed necessary; the decision is about the acceptable balance between welfare harms to individual introduced animals and foreseeable harms to endemic animals and ecosystems. Public attitudes vary strongly by species, perceived invasiveness and whether nonlethal alternatives are credible.

policies.text: targeted lethal control where necessary for major ecological benefit with humane methods
fertility control/nonlethal population management where effective
exclusion/habitat modification before direct killing
no intervention where control harms exceed ecological benefit or repeated killing cannot achieve goals
conservation/ecosystem integrity framework favoring effective population reduction
animal-rights/welfare framework opposing lethal control when less harmful options exist
integrated adaptive management with welfare monitoring and stop/review criteria

cases.title: Wild-animal disease intervention
cases.concise: A free-living carnivore population experiences recurrent rabies outbreaks causing severe neurologic disease and death. An oral vaccination campaign could substantially reduce infection and spillover but would require repeated bait distribution and ecological monitoring. The disease is naturally circulating rather than introduced by a recent human action. The agency must decide whether to vaccinate primarily to reduce wildlife suffering, vaccinate only where conservation or human/animal public-health goals also justify intervention, or leave the natural disease process largely unmanaged except for targeted spillover control.
cases.detailed: For this benchmark, assume oral vaccination is technically effective and does not create a major direct toxicity risk. The main uncertainty concerns ecological effects, recurring costs and the scope of public responsibility for naturally occurring wild-animal suffering. Real programs such as wildlife oral rabies vaccination demonstrate that large-scale intervention is operationally possible, especially for public-health and conservation purposes; they do not establish a professional norm to intervene whenever a natural disease causes animal suffering.

policies.text: vaccinate/intervene when disease threatens public health or conservation and intervention is effective
intervene specifically to reduce severe wild-animal suffering where ecological risk is low
nonintervention when ecological effects of manipulation are too uncertain
targeted intervention in high-burden populations with monitoring rather than ecosystem-wide program
welfare framework favoring preventable suffering reduction
ecological integrity/wildness framework favoring restraint
One Health rule integrating animal welfare, ecosystem effects, and human disease risk

cases.title: Institutional animal-product procurement

cases.title: Adolescent EHR and patient-portal confidentiality
cases.concise: A 16-year-old receives lawful confidential contraception and STI care. A parent appropriately has proxy access to the adolescent's portal for ordinary health information. The current EHR can expose sensitive diagnoses, laboratory results, prescriptions, notes or billing details unless the system applies special protections. The health system must choose how to segment and govern portal access so that confidential information is protected without unnecessarily blocking the adolescent or parent from unrelated records.
cases.detailed: A 16-year-old receives lawful confidential contraception and STI testing during a general adolescent-health visit. The patient has an individual portal account, while a parent retains proxy access for routine pediatric care, appointments, immunizations and other nonconfidential information. The EHR exchanges information with outside clinicians and automatically publishes many test results, medications, problem-list entries and notes. The insurer's explanation-of-benefits workflow can also expose details to the policy holder. The clinical confidentiality rule is not disputed: the sensitive care is protected under the benchmark's stipulated law and policy. The health-system informatics team must decide whether to use granular segmentation and selective proxy blocking across all sensitive data types, rely primarily on clinicians to mark protected items within an otherwise broad proxy-access default, or use a stronger age-based adolescent-control architecture with defined safety/legal exceptions. Any architecture must preserve usable portal access for the adolescent and appropriate parent/guardian access to nonconfidential information.
